  -------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who has trained a classifier or a small neural network, and who wants to know how machines read, translate, transcribe and speak human language, and why the algorithms look the way they do.

**Empirical first**: a bigram model trained on three short sentences assigns probability zero, hence infinite perplexity, to the new sentence “the dog saw the cat”, because one pair of words was never seen ([ch. 1](#ch1)). A recogniser that hears “wreck a nice beach” for “recognise speech” in the six-word sentence “I want to recognise speech today” makes 4 errors, a word error rate of 67 % ([ch. 10](#ch10)).

On synthetic reviews where 40 % of the opinions are negated, a bag-of-words sentiment classifier scores 56 %, and 100 % once the scope of “not” is marked ([ch. 9](#ch9)). Each of these failures has a mathematical cause and an algorithmic fix; the course is the list of those fixes.

The course covers the automatic processing of text and speech: how both are represented, how sequences are modelled (finite-state machines, hidden Markov models, conditional random fields, recurrent networks, transformers), and how the main tasks are solved and evaluated. The tasks are language modelling, machine translation, sentiment analysis, sequence labelling, dialogue, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and code generation with agents.

It shares tools with [Advanced Learning for Text and Graph Data](../s1-altegrad/index.html), [Foundations of Large Language Models](../s1-foundations-llms/index.html) and [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) in semester 1. In semester 2 it runs alongside [Large Language Models for Code and Proof](../s2-llm-code-proof/index.html), [Audio Signal Processing: Time–Frequency Analysis](../s2-audio-time-frequency/index.html) and [Audio Signal Analysis, Indexing and Transformations](../s2-audio-analysis-indexing/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Tokenise text with byte-pair encoding, estimate a smoothed n-gram language model and compute its perplexity.
-   Turn a waveform into log-mel and MFCC features, and justify each step from the source–filter model of speech.
-   Run the forward, Viterbi and Baum–Welch algorithms of a hidden Markov model, and read them as one dynamic program over a semiring.
-   Train a linear-chain conditional random field and evaluate a named-entity tagger with span-level F1.
-   Build word vectors from co-occurrence counts and prove that skip-gram with negative sampling factorises a shifted PMI matrix.
-   Write a transformer block, explain causal masking and the $1/\sqrt{d}$ scaling, and decode from a language model with beam search, temperature or nucleus sampling.
-   Estimate an alignment model for translation by EM, and compute BLEU, WER, Cohen's kappa and pass@k by hand and in code.
-   Derive the CTC loss and its forward recursion, and describe a modern speech synthesis pipeline from text to waveform.
-   Design a retrieval-based or LLM-based dialogue system, and an agent loop with tools.
-   Decide whether a claim of “human parity” is supported, with agreement statistics and a paired bootstrap test.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com presents speech and natural language processing as a subfield of artificial intelligence used in a growing number of applications. The course promises an overview and details of the techniques and tasks of the automatic processing of text and speech.

It names some history of the field, the representation of textual and speech data, language modelling, machine translation, sentiment analysis and other labelling tasks, chatbots, and speech synthesis and recognition. Its aim is to give the key principles, algorithms and mathematics behind the state of the art, and to confront them with the reality of processing real data.

The description announces 9 three-hour slots, each with a lecture of about two hours followed by a quiz and questions. It lists twelve topics, recommends the textbook of Jurafsky and Martin, links a course repository (github.com/rbawden/MVA_2026_SNLP), and states that the instructors will provide readings for each session. The Université Paris-Saclay course detail gives the volume (21 h of lectures) and the type of assessment, with no programme of its own.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: basic linear algebra, calculus, probability theory, and basic machine and deep learning. Ch. 0 reviews the probability, information theory and signal processing that the page uses.

-   **Refreshers** — [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (conditional probability, expectations, maximum likelihood), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (SVD, gradients, Lagrange multipliers) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (every code block).
-   **Semester 1 courses that prepare it** — [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) (backpropagation, RNNs, attention), [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) (EM and hidden Markov models), [Advanced Learning for Text and Graph Data](../s1-altegrad/index.html) (word embeddings, transformers, pretraining), [Foundations of Large Language Models](../s1-foundations-llms/index.html) (training and serving LLMs), [Machine Learning for Time Series](../s1-time-series/index.html) (spectral analysis) and [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html).
-   **Related courses of semester 2** — [Large Language Models for Code and Proof](../s2-llm-code-proof/index.html) (code generation and agents in depth), [Audio Signal Processing: Time–Frequency Analysis](../s2-audio-time-frequency/index.html) and [Audio Signal Analysis, Indexing and Transformations](../s2-audio-analysis-indexing/index.html) (the signal side of ch. 2), [Graphical Models: Discrete Inference and Learning](../s2-graphical-models-discrete/index.html) (inference in chains and beyond), [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) (preference optimisation), [Training and Deploying Large-Scale Models](../s2-training-deploying-large-models/index.html), [Multimodal Explainable AI](../s2-multimodal-xai/index.html) and [Responsible Machine Learning](../s2-responsible-ml/index.html).
-   **After the course** — the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html), for which the project of this course is a rehearsal: read a paper, rerun its code, test a new question.

### Course outline

-   **0. Review** — chain rule of probability, entropy and cross-entropy, the softmax gradient, dynamic programming over semirings, the discrete Fourier transform.
-   **1. Text as data** — a short history of the field, tokens and Zipf's law, byte-pair encoding, n-gram language models, perplexity and smoothing.
-   **2. Speech features** — sampling, the source–filter model, the short-time Fourier transform, the mel filterbank, the cepstrum and MFCCs.
-   **3. Hidden Markov models and finite-state modelling** — weighted automata and transducers, the forward, Viterbi and Baum–Welch algorithms, HMM-based speech recognition.
-   **4. Sequence labelling** — part-of-speech tagging and named entities, the BIO encoding, linear-chain CRFs, neural taggers, span-level evaluation.
-   **5. Word embeddings** — the distributional hypothesis, PMI and SVD, skip-gram with negative sampling as matrix factorisation, subwords, analogies and bias.
-   **6. Deep learning for NLP** — recurrent networks and their gradients, LSTMs, attention, the transformer block.
-   **7. Neural language modelling and LLMs** — neural LMs, pretraining objectives, scaling laws, decoding, instruction tuning and preference optimisation.
-   **8. Machine translation** — from rules to IBM models, neural translation with beam search, BLEU and learned metrics.
-   **9. Sentiment analysis** — polarity and aspects, naive Bayes and logistic regression, negation and compositionality.
-   **10. Speech recognition and synthesis** — WER, CTC, encoder–decoders and self-supervised speech; text-to-speech pipelines and vocoders.
-   **11. Chatbots, code generation and agents** — from ELIZA to LLM assistants, retrieval-augmented generation, pass@k, tool-using agents.
-   **12. Evaluation** — agreement between humans, human-parity claims, significance testing, benchmark pitfalls.
-   **13. Complements** — Kneser–Ney smoothing, the derivation of Baum–Welch, the RNN transducer, the KL-regularised optimum behind DPO (self-study).
-   **14. Research directions and open problems** — spoken language models without text, efficient long-context architectures, multilingual and document-level translation, evaluation, affective interaction (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session; it is short, and every later chapter uses cross-entropy and dynamic programming.
-   Follow one thread across the course: the same dynamic program computes an HMM likelihood (ch. 3), a CRF partition function (ch. 4), the CTC loss (ch. 10) and an edit distance (ch. 10). Rewrite it once in each semiring.
-   After each session, do the exercises of its row, then run the code of the chapter and change one parameter; the printed numbers are quoted in the text, so you can check your environment.
-   The code needs Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and PyTorch (CPU); every block uses synthetic or hand-written data and runs in a few seconds. No download is needed.
-   Keep a one-page sheet with the definitions of perplexity, BLEU, WER, span F1, kappa and pass@k: the quizzes test whether you can compute them quickly.
-   Start the project early: pick a paper with code in week 2, as the official assessment requires a one-page plan before the results.

## 0. Review: probability, information, dynamic programming and the Fourier transform {#ch0}

Every chapter of the course manipulates probabilities of sequences, measures models by a cross-entropy, trains them through a softmax, and computes sums over exponentially many paths with a dynamic program. This review states these tools once, with proofs, and adds the discrete Fourier transform needed for speech in ch. 2.

### 0.1 Probabilities of sequences

A sentence is a sequence of tokens $w_1, \dots, w_n$ drawn from a finite vocabulary $V$. Any joint law factorises by the chain rule:
$$
P(w_1, \dots, w_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} P(w_t \mid w_1, \dots, w_{t-1}).
$$

The factorisation is exact; models differ by how they approximate each conditional. A Markov model of order $k$ keeps only the last $k$ tokens (ch. 1, ch. 3); a recurrent network or a transformer keeps a learned summary of the whole prefix (ch. 6, ch. 7).

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Entropy, cross-entropy, Kullback–Leibler divergence]{.tag} For two laws $p, q$ on a finite set $V$, with $q > 0$ where $p > 0$:
$$
H(p) = -\sum_{w} p(w) \log p(w), \qquad H(p, q) = -\sum_{w} p(w) \log q(w),
$$
$$
\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_{w} p(w) \log \frac{p(w)}{q(w)} = H(p, q) - H(p).
$$

With the natural logarithm the unit is the nat; with $\log_2$ it is the bit.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Gibbs' inequality]{.tag} For all laws $p, q$ on $V$,
$$
H(p, q) \geq H(p),
$$
with equality if and only if $q = p$ on the support of $p$.

::: proof
On the support $S$ of $p$, apply Jensen's inequality to the concave logarithm:
$$
-\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_{w \in S} p(w) \log \frac{q(w)}{p(w)} \leq \log \sum_{w \in S} q(w) \leq \log 1 = 0 .
$$

Equality in Jensen requires the ratio $q/p$ to be constant on $S$, and equality in the second step requires $q(S) = 1$; together they give $q = p$ on $S$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Consequence: minimising the expected negative log-likelihood of a model $q$ under the data law $p$ is the same as minimising $\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q)$. This is why every model of the course is trained with a cross-entropy, and why no model can do better than the entropy of the source (Proposition 7.2).

### 0.2 Softmax and its gradient

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Softmax]{.tag} For scores $z \in \mathbb{R}^K$ (the *logits*) and a temperature $T > 0$,
$$
\mathrm{softmax}(z / T)_k = \frac{e^{z_k / T}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j / T}} .
$$

Adding the same constant to every logit leaves the result unchanged; implementations subtract $\max_j z_j$ before exponentiating, to avoid overflow.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Gradient of the softmax cross-entropy]{.tag} Let $p = \mathrm{softmax}(z)$ and let $y$ be the index of the correct class. The loss $\ell(z) = -\log p_y$ has gradient
$$
\nabla_z \ell = p - e_y ,
$$
where $e_y$ is the one-hot vector of $y$.

::: proof
Write $\ell(z) = -z_y + \log \sum_j e^{z_j}$. The derivative of the first term in $z_k$ is $-\mathbf{1}[k = y]$; the derivative of the log-sum-exp is $e^{z_k} / \sum_j e^{z_j} = p_k$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The gradient is the difference between what the model predicts and what was observed. The same shape, “expected features minus observed features”, returns for conditional random fields in Theorem 4.4.

### 0.3 Dynamic programming over a semiring

Many quantities of the course are sums, over exponentially many paths, of products of local weights. They are computed in polynomial time because the sum distributes over the product.

::: def
[Definition 0.5 — Semiring]{.tag} A semiring $(\mathbb{K}, \oplus, \otimes, \bar 0, \bar 1)$ is a set with two associative operations, an addition and a multiplication, such that:

-   the addition $\oplus$ is commutative, with neutral element $\bar 0$;
-   the multiplication $\otimes$ has neutral element $\bar 1$ and distributes over $\oplus$;
-   $\bar 0$ annihilates: $\bar 0 \otimes a = \bar 0$.

The four semirings of the course:

| Name | Set | $\oplus$ | $\otimes$ | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | $[0, \infty)$ | $+$ | $\times$ | likelihoods (forward algorithm) |
| Viterbi | $[0, 1]$ | $\max$ | $\times$ | best path |
| Log | $\mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty\}$ | log-sum-exp | $+$ | stable likelihoods, CRFs, CTC |
| Tropical | $\mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ | $\min$ | $+$ | edit distance, shortest paths |
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.6 — Path sums in a layered graph]{.tag} Let a graph have layers $0, \dots, T$ of at most $K$ nodes, a weight $w(e) \in \mathbb{K}$ on each edge between consecutive layers, and define the weight of a path as the $\otimes$-product of its edges. Then the $\oplus$-sum of the weights of all paths from layer 0 to layer $T$ is computed by
$$
\alpha_0(s) = \bar 1 \ \text{ for each node } s \text{ of layer } 0, \qquad \alpha_t(j) = \bigoplus_{i} \alpha_{t-1}(i) \otimes w(i \to j),
$$
followed by the sum over the last layer:
$$
\bigoplus_{j} \alpha_T(j) .
$$

This costs $O(T K^2)$ operations, against $K^T$ paths.

::: proof
By induction on $t$: $\alpha_t(j)$ is the $\oplus$-sum of the weights of all paths ending at node $j$ of layer $t$.

A path to $j$ is a path to some node $i$ of the previous layer followed by the edge $i \to j$. Commutativity and associativity of $\oplus$ let us group the paths by this node $i$. Distributivity then turns the sum over the paths through $i$ into
$$
\alpha_{t-1}(i) \otimes w(i \to j) .
$$

Each layer costs at most $K^2$ products. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 0.4 The discrete Fourier transform

::: def
[Definition 0.7 — Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)]{.tag} For $x \in \mathbb{C}^N$,
$$
X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n\, e^{-2 i \pi k n / N}, \qquad k = 0, \dots, N-1 .
$$

For a signal sampled at $f_s$ hertz, bin $k$ corresponds to the frequency $k f_s / N$. The fast Fourier transform computes all $X_k$ in $O(N \log N)$ operations.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.8 — Convolution theorem]{.tag} If $y = x \circledast h$ is the circular convolution, $y_n = \sum_m x_m h_{(n - m) \bmod N}$, then
$$
Y_k = X_k\, H_k \quad \text{for every } k .
$$

::: proof
Substitute and set $r = (n - m) \bmod N$; the exponential factorises because $e^{-2 i \pi k n / N}$ is $N$-periodic in $n$:
$$
Y_k = \sum_{m} x_m e^{-2 i \pi k m / N} \sum_{r} h_r e^{-2 i \pi k r / N} = X_k H_k .
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Ch. 2 uses this with a logarithm: a convolution becomes a product in frequency, and a sum after taking $\log |\cdot|$.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   The chain rule factorises any law on sequences; models differ by what they keep of the prefix.
-   Cross-entropy is at least the entropy (Gibbs), so training by negative log-likelihood minimises a KL divergence.
-   The gradient of the softmax cross-entropy is “predicted minus observed”.
-   One dynamic program, run in different semirings, computes likelihoods, best paths and edit distances in $O(TK^2)$.
-   The DFT turns convolutions into products; its bin $k$ is the frequency $k f_s / N$.
:::

## 1. Text as data: a short history, tokenisation and n-gram language models {#ch1}

Before any model, text must be cut into units, and the units given probabilities. This chapter places the field in its history, defines subword tokens, and builds the oldest language model still used as a baseline: the smoothed n-gram, measured by perplexity.

### 1.1 A short history

The field alternated between hand-written rules and statistics learned from data.

-   **1948–1966, rules and first statistics.** Shannon generated English-like text from n-gram counts (1948). The 1954 Georgetown–IBM demonstration translated some sixty Russian sentences with a few rules; the 1966 ALPAC report judged translation disappointing.
-   **1975–2010, statistics.** Hidden Markov models took over speech recognition (ch. 3); the same noisy-channel view produced statistical translation at IBM (ch. 8).
-   **2003–2017, neural models.** A neural language model (2003), deep acoustic models (around 2012), word2vec (2013), attention (2015), the transformer (2017).
-   **2018–today, pretraining at scale.** One pretrained model became the starting point of every task, and instruction-tuned assistants appeared in 2022 (ch. 7).

### 1.2 Tokens and subwords

A *token* is an occurrence of a unit in a text; a *type* is a distinct unit. Word frequencies follow Zipf's law: the $r$-th most frequent type has frequency roughly proportional to $1/r$. Many types occur once, so any fixed word vocabulary meets unseen words at test time.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Tokeniser]{.tag} A tokeniser maps a string to a sequence of symbols of a finite vocabulary $V$, and back. Byte-level tokenisers never meet an unknown symbol but give long sequences; word-level ones give short sequences with unknown words; subword tokenisers sit in between.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Byte-pair encoding (BPE)]{.tag} Start from characters, with an end-of-word marker. Repeat a fixed number of times: count the pairs of adjacent symbols, weighted by word frequency, and merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol. The ordered list of merges is the tokeniser; it segments a new word by replaying the merges (Sennrich, Haddow and Birch, 2016a).
:::

::: ex
[Code 1.3 — Learning BPE merges]{.tag}

```python
from collections import Counter

def learn_bpe(word_counts, n_merges):
    """Byte-pair encoding: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols."""
    vocab = {tuple(w) + ("</w>",): c for w, c in word_counts.items()}
    merges = []
    for _ in range(n_merges):
        pairs = Counter()
        for symbols, c in vocab.items():
            for pair in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
                pairs[pair] += c
        (a, b), freq = pairs.most_common(1)[0]        # ties: first pair seen
        merges.append((a + b, freq))
        new_vocab = {}
        for symbols, c in vocab.items():
            out, i = [], 0
            while i < len(symbols):
                if symbols[i:i + 2] == (a, b):
                    out.append(a + b); i += 2
                else:
                    out.append(symbols[i]); i += 1
            new_vocab[tuple(out)] = c
        vocab = new_vocab
    return merges, vocab

counts = {"low": 5, "lower": 2, "newest": 6, "widest": 3}
merges, vocab = learn_bpe(counts, 5)
print(merges)
for symbols, c in vocab.items():
    print(c, " ".join(symbols))
```

The five merges are `es`, `est`, `est</w>`, `lo` and `low`. The superlative suffix becomes one symbol, so the unseen word “lowest” is segmented as `low` + `est</w>`.
:::

### 1.3 n-gram language models and perplexity

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — n-gram language model]{.tag} An n-gram model assumes that each token depends only on the $n - 1$ previous ones. A sentence is padded with $n - 1$ start symbols `<s>` and an end symbol `</s>`, and
$$
P(w_1, \dots, w_m) = \prod_{t=1}^{m+1} P(w_t \mid w_{t-n+1}, \dots, w_{t-1}) .
$$

For $n = 2$ (bigrams), the parameters are the conditional laws $P(w \mid u)$ for each context word $u$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.5 — Maximum likelihood estimate]{.tag} Let $c(u, w)$ count the bigram $u\,w$ in the training corpus and $c(u) = \sum_w c(u, w)$. The bigram model of maximal likelihood is
$$
\hat P(w \mid u) = \frac{c(u, w)}{c(u)} .
$$

::: proof
The log-likelihood is a sum of independent terms, one per context $u$:
$$
\sum_u \sum_w c(u, w) \log P(w \mid u) = -\sum_u c(u)\, H\Big(\frac{c(u, \cdot)}{c(u)},\, P(\cdot \mid u)\Big).
$$

Each cross-entropy is minimal when the model law equals the empirical law, by Gibbs' inequality (Proposition 0.2). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Perplexity]{.tag} The perplexity of a model $P$ on a test text of $N$ predicted tokens is the exponential of its average negative log-likelihood:

::: key
[Key result — perplexity]{.tag}
$$
\mathrm{PP} = \exp\Big( -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \log P(w_t \mid w_{<t}) \Big)
$$
:::

A uniform model over $V$ has perplexity $|V|$: perplexity is an effective number of equally likely choices per token. It compares models only under the same tokenisation.
:::

The maximum likelihood estimate gives probability zero, hence infinite perplexity, to any test text with an unseen bigram. Smoothing moves some mass to unseen events.

::: def
[Definition 1.7 — Add-k smoothing]{.tag} For $k > 0$,
$$
P_k(w \mid u) = \frac{c(u, w) + k}{c(u) + k\, |V|} .
$$

With $k = 1$ it is Laplace smoothing. Kneser–Ney smoothing, which does better, is in ch. 13.
:::

::: ex
[Code 1.8 — Perplexity of unigram and bigram models]{.tag}

```python
import math
from collections import Counter

train = ["<s> the cat sat on the mat </s>", "<s> the dog sat on the log </s>",
         "<s> the cat saw the dog </s>"]
test = ["<s> the dog sat on the mat </s>", "<s> the dog saw the cat </s>"]   # "dog saw" is unseen
tok = [s.split() for s in train]
V = sorted({w for s in tok for w in s} - {"<s>"})     # predicted vocabulary (|V| = 9)
uni = Counter(w for s in tok for w in s[1:])
big = Counter((u, w) for s in tok for u, w in zip(s, s[1:]))
ctx = Counter(u for s in tok for u in s[:-1])

def p_bigram(w, u, k):
    """Add-k smoothed bigram probability P(w | u)."""
    return (big[u, w] + k) / (ctx[u] + k * len(V))

def perplexity(sents, logp):
    lp, n = 0.0, 0
    for s in sents:
        w = s.split()
        for u, v in zip(w, w[1:]):
            lp += logp(v, u); n += 1
    return math.exp(-lp / n)

N = sum(uni.values())
print("unigram (MLE)   ", round(perplexity(test, lambda w, u: math.log(uni[w] / N)), 2))
mle = lambda w, u: math.log(big[u, w] / ctx[u]) if big[u, w] else -math.inf
print("bigram (MLE)    ", perplexity(test, mle))
for k in [1.0, 0.1, 0.01]:
    print(f"bigram add-{k:<5}", round(perplexity(test, lambda w, u: math.log(p_bigram(w, u, k))), 2))
```

The unigram model has perplexity 7.45; the unsmoothed bigram model, infinite. Add-k smoothing gives 5.17 for $k = 1$, 3.25 for $k = 0.1$ and 3.65 for $k = 0.01$: too much smoothing flattens the model, too little starves the unseen bigram, so $k$ is tuned on held-out data.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   The field swung from rules to statistics to neural networks.
-   Zipf's law guarantees unseen words; subword tokenisers such as BPE remove them.
-   The n-gram MLE is a table of relative counts (Proposition 1.5); it must be smoothed.
-   Perplexity is the exponential of the per-token cross-entropy; it compares models under one tokenisation.
:::

## 2. Speech features and signal processing {#ch2}

A recogniser reads one feature vector every 10 ms, which keeps what distinguishes speech sounds and drops the rest, such as pitch. This chapter derives the classical pipeline, from sampling to MFCCs, from a model of speech production.

### 2.1 Sampling and the source–filter model

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Sampled signal]{.tag} A signal $x(t)$ sampled at rate $f_s$ gives $x_n = x(n / f_s)$. By the Shannon sampling theorem, it is recoverable from its samples if it has no energy above $f_s / 2$. Speech corpora usually use 16 kHz, telephone speech 8 kHz.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — Source–filter model]{.tag} Over a few tens of milliseconds, speech is an excitation $e$ filtered by the vocal tract, of impulse response $h$:
$$
s = e * h .
$$

For vowels, $e$ is a train of glottal pulses at the fundamental frequency $f_0$, roughly 80 to 250 Hz for adults; for sounds such as /s/, it is noise. The resonances of the tract, the *formants*, identify the vowel: /a/ has formants near 700 and 1100–1200 Hz.
:::

The phoneme is carried by $h$, the pitch by $e$. A good feature keeps the spectral envelope ($h$) and discards the harmonic fine structure ($e$).

### 2.2 The short-time Fourier transform

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — STFT and spectrogram]{.tag} Cut the signal into frames of $L$ samples every $R$ samples, multiply each frame by a window $w$ (Hamming or Hann), and take a DFT of size $N \geq L$ (Definition 0.7):
$$
X_m(k) = \sum_{n=0}^{L-1} x_{mR + n}\, w_n\, e^{-2 i \pi k n / N} .
$$

The power spectrogram is $|X_m(k)|^2$. The standard choice, $L = 25$ ms and $R = 10$ ms, is short enough for the tract to be stationary and long enough to hold two or three pitch periods. A *pre-emphasis* filter $x_n - 0.97\, x_{n-1}$ is often applied first, to lift high frequencies.
:::

### 2.3 The mel filterbank

Pitch perception is roughly linear below 1 kHz and logarithmic above; the mel scale imitates it.

::: def
[Definition 2.4 — Mel scale and log-mel energies]{.tag} The mel scale is
$$
\mathrm{mel}(f) = 2595 \log_{10}\Big(1 + \frac{f}{700}\Big),
$$
so that $\mathrm{mel}(1000) \approx 1000$. Place $M$ triangular filters $F_j$ with centres equally spaced in mel up to $f_s / 2$, each spanning the centres of its two neighbours. The log-mel energies of frame $m$ are
$$
E_m(j) = \log \sum_{k} F_j(k)\, |X_m(k)|^2, \qquad j = 1, \dots, M,
$$
with $M = 40$ or $80$ in practice.
:::

### 2.4 The cepstrum and MFCCs

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — The logarithm separates source and filter]{.tag} Under the model of Definition 2.2, treated as a circular convolution within one frame,
$$
\log |S_k| = \log |E_k| + \log |H_k| \quad \text{for every bin } k .
$$

The *cepstrum*, the inverse DFT of $\log |S_k|$, is the sum of the cepstra of $e$ and $h$. The smooth envelope $\log |H_k|$ occupies the low *quefrencies*; the harmonic comb $\log |E_k|$ produces a peak at the pitch period $1 / f_0$.

::: proof
The convolution theorem (Proposition 0.8) gives $S_k = E_k H_k$; take moduli and logarithms, and use the linearity of the inverse DFT. A slowly varying function of $k$ has its inverse DFT near quefrency 0; a comb of spacing $f_0$ has it at multiples of $1 / f_0$. Windowing makes the separation approximate. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCC)]{.tag} The MFCCs of frame $m$ are the first coefficients, usually 13, of the type-II discrete cosine transform of the log-mel energies:
$$
c_m(q) = \sum_{j=1}^{M} E_m(j) \cos\Big(\frac{\pi q (j - 1/2)}{M}\Big), \qquad q = 0, \dots, 12 .
$$

They are the low-quefrency part of a mel-warped cepstrum: they describe the envelope (Proposition 2.5), and they are nearly decorrelated, which suited the diagonal Gaussians of HMM recognisers (ch. 3). Time differences (*deltas*) are often appended.
:::

::: ex
[Code 2.7 — From a waveform to log-mel features and MFCCs]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import dct

sr = 16000
t = np.arange(sr // 2) / sr                         # 0.5 s of a synthetic vowel /a/
f0, formants = 120.0, np.array([700.0, 1220.0, 2600.0])
x = np.zeros_like(t)
for h in range(1, 60):                              # harmonics of f0 shaped by formants
    gain = np.exp(-0.5 * ((h * f0 - formants) / 100.0) ** 2) @ [1.0, 0.8, 0.3]
    x += gain * np.sin(2 * np.pi * h * f0 * t)
x += 0.01 * np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=x.size)

def hz_to_mel(f): return 2595 * np.log10(1 + f / 700)
def mel_to_hz(m): return 700 * (10 ** (m / 2595) - 1)

def log_mel(x, sr, n_fft=512, win=400, hop=160, n_mels=40):
    x = np.append(x[0], x[1:] - 0.97 * x[:-1])                         # pre-emphasis
    n_frames = 1 + (len(x) - win) // hop
    frames = np.stack([x[i * hop: i * hop + win] for i in range(n_frames)]) * np.hamming(win)
    power = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(frames, n_fft)) ** 2 / n_fft           # (frames, 257)
    edges = mel_to_hz(np.linspace(0, hz_to_mel(sr / 2), n_mels + 2))   # triangle corners
    bins = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_fft, 1 / sr)
    fb = np.zeros((n_mels, bins.size))
    for m in range(n_mels):
        lo, c, hi = edges[m: m + 3]
        fb[m] = np.clip(np.minimum((bins - lo) / (c - lo), (hi - bins) / (hi - c)), 0, None)
    return np.log(power @ fb.T + 1e-10), edges[1:-1]

L, centres = log_mel(x, sr)
mfcc = dct(L, type=2, norm="ortho", axis=1)[:, :13]                    # keep 13 cepstra
print("log-mel", L.shape, "MFCC", mfcc.shape)
avg = L.mean(0)
peaks = [m for m in range(1, 39) if avg[m] > avg[m - 1] and avg[m] > avg[m + 1]]
print("peaks of the mel spectrum at", np.round(centres[peaks]).astype(int), "Hz")
```

Half a second gives 48 frames of 40 log-mel energies and 13 MFCCs. The mel spectrum peaks near 764, 1171 and 2554 Hz, the three formants. Two weak bumps near 92 and 195 Hz are not harmonics, which have almost no energy there, but window leakage sampled unevenly by the lowest filters, only three or four DFT bins wide.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.8 — Orders of magnitude]{.tag} At 16 kHz, a 25 ms window holds 400 samples and a 10 ms hop is 160 samples. One second of speech gives
$$
1 + \lfloor (16000 - 400) / 160 \rfloor = 98 \text{ frames}.
$$

A DFT of size 512 has bins every $16000 / 512 = 31.25$ Hz; a pitch period at 120 Hz lasts 8.3 ms, so three fit in a window.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Speech is an excitation (pitch or noise) filtered by the vocal tract (formants); the phoneme lives in the filter.
-   The STFT with 25 ms windows every 10 ms gives about 100 frames per second.
-   Log-mel energies warp frequency like hearing; they are the standard input of neural recognisers (ch. 10).
-   The logarithm turns the source–filter convolution into a sum; the DCT keeps the envelope in 13 MFCCs.
:::

## 3. Hidden Markov models and finite-state modelling {#ch3}

Speech frames are produced by a hidden sequence of sounds, and words by a hidden sequence of tags. Finite-state machines and hidden Markov models describe such hidden sequences; three dynamic programs make them usable: likelihood, best path and learning.

### 3.1 Weighted finite-state machines

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Weighted finite-state transducer (WFST)]{.tag} A WFST over a semiring $\mathbb{K}$ (Definition 0.5) has a finite set of states, an initial state, final states, and weighted transitions
$$
p \xrightarrow{\ a \,:\, b \,/\, w\ } q
$$
that read an input symbol $a$, write an output symbol $b$ (possibly empty) and carry a weight $w \in \mathbb{K}$.

The weight of a pair of strings is the $\oplus$-sum, over the accepting paths that read the first and write the second, of the $\otimes$-product of their weights.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.2 — Composition]{.tag} The composition $T_1 \circ T_2$ maps $x$ to $z$ with weight
$$
(T_1 \circ T_2)(x, z) = \bigoplus_{y} T_1(x, y) \otimes T_2(y, z) .
$$

Its states are pairs of states; a transition of $T_1$ writing $y$ is matched with one of $T_2$ reading $y$.
:::

A recogniser composes four transducers (Mohri, Pereira and Riley, 2002): HMM states to context-dependent phones ($H$), to phones ($C$), to words through the pronunciation lexicon ($L$), and the n-gram grammar of ch. 1 ($G$). Decoding searches the best path of $H \circ C \circ L \circ G$ in the tropical semiring.

### 3.2 Hidden Markov models

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — Hidden Markov model]{.tag} An HMM with $K$ hidden states has an initial law $\pi$, a transition matrix $A$ with rows summing to one, and emission laws $b_j$. A hidden path $q_1, \dots, q_T$ and observations $o_1, \dots, o_T$ have joint probability
$$
P(q, o) = \pi_{q_1} b_{q_1}(o_1) \prod_{t=2}^{T} A_{q_{t-1} q_t}\, b_{q_t}(o_t) .
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — Forward algorithm]{.tag} Let $\alpha_t(j) = P(o_1, \dots, o_t, q_t = j)$. Then $\alpha_1(j) = \pi_j b_j(o_1)$,

::: key
[Key result — the forward recursion]{.tag}
$$
\alpha_t(j) = \Big( \sum_{i=1}^{K} \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, A_{ij} \Big)\, b_j(o_t), \qquad P(o_1, \dots, o_T) = \sum_{j} \alpha_T(j),
$$
:::

and the likelihood costs $O(T K^2)$ operations instead of $K^T$ terms.

::: proof
The joint law of Definition 3.3 is a product of edge weights along a path in a layered graph with $K$ states per step. Apply Proposition 0.6 in the probability semiring, then sum over the last state. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.5 — Viterbi algorithm]{.tag} Let $\delta_t(j)$ be the largest joint probability of a path ending in state $j$ at time $t$. Then
$$
\delta_t(j) = \max_{i} \delta_{t-1}(i)\, A_{ij}\, b_j(o_t),
$$
and back-pointers to the maximising $i$, read backwards from $\arg\max_j \delta_T(j)$, give the best path.

::: proof
Same graph, in the Viterbi semiring, where $\max$ distributes over products of non-negative numbers. A prefix of an optimal path is optimal among the paths reaching the same state, so the back-pointers recover an optimal path. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Code 3.6 — Forward and Viterbi, checked by brute force]{.tag}

```python
import itertools
import numpy as np

pi = np.array([0.8, 0.2])                        # states: 0 = hot, 1 = cold
A = np.array([[0.6, 0.4], [0.5, 0.5]])           # A[i, j] = P(q_t = j | q_{t-1} = i)
B = np.array([[0.2, 0.4, 0.4], [0.5, 0.4, 0.1]]) # B[i, o] = P(o | i), o = 1, 2, 3 ice creams
obs = [2, 0, 2]                                  # observed 3, 1, 3 (0-based symbols)

def forward(obs):
    alpha = pi * B[:, obs[0]]
    for o in obs[1:]:
        alpha = (alpha @ A) * B[:, o]            # O(K^2) per step
    return alpha.sum()

def viterbi(obs):
    delta, back = np.log(pi * B[:, obs[0]]), []
    for o in obs[1:]:
        scores = delta[:, None] + np.log(A)      # scores[i, j]: best path ending i -> j
        back.append(scores.argmax(0))
        delta = scores.max(0) + np.log(B[:, o])
    path = [int(delta.argmax())]
    for bp in reversed(back):
        path.insert(0, int(bp[path[0]]))
    return path, np.exp(delta.max())

def joint(q, obs):
    p = pi[q[0]] * B[q[0], obs[0]]
    for t in range(1, len(obs)):
        p *= A[q[t - 1], q[t]] * B[q[t], obs[t]]
    return p

paths = list(itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=len(obs)))
print("P(O): forward", round(forward(obs), 6), " brute force", round(sum(joint(q, obs) for q in paths), 6))
best = max(paths, key=lambda q: joint(q, obs))
path, p = viterbi(obs)
print("Viterbi", path, round(p, 6), " brute force", list(best), round(joint(best, obs), 6))
```

Both methods give $P(O) = 0.028562$ and the best path hot, cold, hot with probability $0.0128$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.7 — The same numbers by hand]{.tag} For the observations 3, 1, 3:

-   $\alpha_1 = (0.8 \cdot 0.4,\ 0.2 \cdot 0.1) = (0.32,\ 0.02)$;
-   the second step mixes the two states, then emits “1”:
    $$
    \alpha_2 = \big( (0.32 \cdot 0.6 + 0.02 \cdot 0.5) \cdot 0.2,\ (0.32 \cdot 0.4 + 0.02 \cdot 0.5) \cdot 0.5 \big) = (0.0404,\ 0.069);
    $$
-   $\alpha_3 = (0.023496,\ 0.005066)$, whose sum is the likelihood:
$$
P(O) = 0.028562 .
$$

Viterbi replaces sums by maxima: $\delta_2 = (0.0384,\ 0.064)$, then $\delta_3(\text{hot}) = 0.064 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.4 = 0.0128$, from “cold”.
:::

### 3.3 Learning: the Baum–Welch algorithm

Without observed states, parameters are learned by EM. The backward variables $\beta_t(i) = P(o_{t+1}, \dots, o_T \mid q_t = i)$ satisfy the mirror recursion
$$
\beta_t(i) = \sum_j A_{ij}\, b_j(o_{t+1})\, \beta_{t+1}(j), \qquad \beta_T(i) = 1 .
$$

They give the posteriors of one state and of one transition:
$$
\gamma_t(i) = \frac{\alpha_t(i) \beta_t(i)}{P(O)}, \qquad \xi_t(i, j) = \frac{\alpha_t(i) A_{ij} b_j(o_{t+1}) \beta_{t+1}(j)}{P(O)} .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.8 — Baum–Welch re-estimation]{.tag} The updates
$$
\pi_i \leftarrow \gamma_1(i), \qquad A_{ij} \leftarrow \frac{\sum_{t<T} \xi_t(i, j)}{\sum_{t<T} \gamma_t(i)}, \qquad b_i(v) \leftarrow \frac{\sum_{t : o_t = v} \gamma_t(i)}{\sum_{t} \gamma_t(i)}
$$
never decrease the likelihood $P(O)$.

::: proof
This is EM. The E-step computes the posteriors; the M-step maximises the expected complete log-likelihood, which splits into one multinomial estimate per row, with fractional counts (Proposition 1.5). EM raises a lower bound of $\log P(O)$ that is tight at the current parameters, so the likelihood cannot decrease. Derivation and code: [ch. 13](#ch13), 13.2. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 3.4 HMM-based speech recognition

::: def
[Definition 3.9 — The noisy channel for recognition]{.tag} Given acoustic frames $O$, the recogniser outputs
$$
\hat W = \arg\max_{W} P(O \mid W)\, P(W),
$$
an acoustic model times a language model (ch. 1). Each phone is a three-state left-to-right HMM; words and sentences are paths in the composed graph of section 3.1.
:::

The emissions were Gaussian mixtures over MFCCs until about 2010. Hybrid systems then used a neural network predicting the state posterior $P(q \mid o_t)$, divided by the prior $P(q)$ to give a scaled likelihood. Ch. 10 removes the HMM altogether.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   WFSTs are weighted relations between strings; composition chains acoustics, lexicon and grammar.
-   Forward, Viterbi and backward are one dynamic program in the probability or Viterbi semiring, in $O(TK^2)$.
-   Baum–Welch is EM: posteriors from forward–backward, then fractional-count estimates; the likelihood never decreases.
-   Recognition is $\arg\max_W P(O \mid W) P(W)$; neural networks entered as emission models before replacing the HMM.
:::

## 4. Sequence labelling {#ch4}

Many tasks give one label per token: a part of speech, an entity type, a slot of a request. This chapter encodes spans as tags, replaces the HMM tagger by a discriminative conditional random field, and scores taggers by spans.

### 4.1 Tasks and the BIO encoding

Part-of-speech tagging assigns each word a category such as noun or verb (17 in the Universal Dependencies tag set). Named-entity recognition finds spans naming persons, organisations or locations; CoNLL-2003 (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003) uses four types.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — BIO encoding]{.tag} A set of non-overlapping typed spans is encoded with one tag per token: `B-X` opens a span of type X, `I-X` continues it, and `O` marks tokens outside every span. For example:

| Ada | Lovelace | was | born | in | London | . |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `B-PER` | `I-PER` | `O` | `O` | `O` | `B-LOC` | `O` |

A tag `I-X` may only follow `B-X` or `I-X`; decoders forbid the other transitions.
:::

An HMM tagger (ch. 3) must generate every word, so it cannot easily use overlapping clues such as capitalisation, suffixes or the next word.

### 4.2 Linear-chain conditional random fields

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — Linear-chain CRF]{.tag} Given a sentence $x$ of length $T$ and feature functions $f(y_{t-1}, y_t, x, t) \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a CRF with weights $\theta$ defines
$$
p_\theta(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z_\theta(x)} \exp\Big( \sum_{t=1}^{T} \theta^\top f(y_{t-1}, y_t, x, t) \Big),
$$
where $Z_\theta(x)$ sums the numerator over all $K^T$ tag sequences (Lafferty, McCallum and Pereira, 2001).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — Inference in a CRF]{.tag} $Z_\theta(x)$, the marginals $p_\theta(y_t \mid x)$ and the best sequence $\arg\max_y p_\theta(y \mid x)$ are computed in $O(TK^2)$.

::: proof
Each sequence is a path in a layered graph with edge weights $\exp(\theta^\top f(y_{t-1}, y_t, x, t))$. Proposition 0.6 gives $Z$; forward and backward passes give the marginals (ch. 3); the Viterbi semiring gives the best path. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Gradient and concavity of the CRF likelihood]{.tag} For a training pair $(x, y)$, the log-likelihood $\ell(\theta) = \log p_\theta(y \mid x)$ is concave, with gradient
$$
\nabla \ell(\theta) = \sum_{t} f(y_{t-1}, y_t, x, t) - \mathbb{E}_{y' \sim p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)} \Big[ \sum_t f(y'_{t-1}, y'_t, x, t) \Big] .
$$

::: proof
Write $F(y') = \sum_t f(y'_{t-1}, y'_t, x, t)$, so that $\ell(\theta) = \theta^\top F(y) - \log Z_\theta(x)$. Differentiating the log-sum-exp, as in Proposition 0.4, gives the expectation of $F$ under $p_\theta$.

The Hessian of $\log Z_\theta$ is the covariance matrix of $F(y')$ under $p_\theta$, which is positive semi-definite, so $\ell$ is concave. The expectation needs only the pairwise marginals, given by forward–backward. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

At the optimum, expected feature counts equal observed ones, as for logistic regression.

::: ex
[Code 4.5 — The forward algorithm computes log Z, and its gradient gives the marginals]{.tag}

```python
import itertools
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(1); torch.manual_seed(0)
T, K = 5, 3                                      # 5 tokens, tags {O, B, I}
E = torch.randn(T, K, requires_grad=True)        # emission scores psi_t(y_t) = w . f(x, t, y_t)
W = torch.randn(K, K)                            # transition scores between consecutive tags

def log_partition(E, W):
    """Forward algorithm in the log semiring: log of the sum over all K^T tag sequences."""
    a = E[0]
    for t in range(1, len(E)):
        a = torch.logsumexp(a[:, None] + W, dim=0) + E[t]
    return torch.logsumexp(a, dim=0)

def score(y):
    return E[torch.arange(T), y].sum() + W[y[:-1], y[1:]].sum()

logZ = log_partition(E, W)
seqs = torch.tensor(list(itertools.product(range(K), repeat=T)))     # 243 sequences
brute = torch.logsumexp(torch.stack([score(y) for y in seqs]), 0)
print("log Z forward", round(logZ.item(), 4), " brute force", round(brute.item(), 4))

logZ.backward()                                  # d log Z / d E[t, k] = P(y_t = k | x)
probs = torch.softmax(torch.stack([score(y) for y in seqs]).detach(), 0)
marg = torch.stack([probs[seqs[:, 2] == k].sum() for k in range(K)])
print("gradient at t=2", E.grad[2].numpy().round(4), " marginals", marg.numpy().round(4))
```

Both computations give $\log Z = 7.3242$, and the gradient of $\log Z$ with respect to the scores of token 3 equals its marginals (0.4238, 0.3264, 0.2497): differentiating the forward algorithm *is* the backward pass.
:::

### 4.3 Neural taggers, a preview of ch. 6–7

A bidirectional LSTM (ch. 6) can produce the emission scores of a CRF layer (Lample and coauthors, 2016). With a pretrained transformer (ch. 7), a linear layer on each token's representation often suffices; a word split into subwords takes the label of its first subword.

### 4.4 Evaluation by spans

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Span-level precision, recall and F1]{.tag} A predicted span counts as correct only if its boundaries and its type match a gold span exactly. With $c$ correct spans, $p$ predicted and $g$ gold:
$$
P = \frac{c}{p}, \qquad R = \frac{c}{g}, \qquad F_1 = \frac{2 P R}{P + R} .
$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.7 — Token accuracy hides span errors]{.tag} The gold tags of “Ada Lovelace was born in London .” contain two spans. A tagger that outputs `B-PER O O O O B-LOC O` is right on 6 tokens out of 7, an accuracy of 86 %. It finds one span out of two, and predicts one wrong span (“Ada” alone), so $P = R = 1/2$ and
$$
F_1 = 0.5 .
$$
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   BIO tags turn span extraction into one label per token.
-   A linear-chain CRF is a log-linear model over whole tag sequences; forward–backward gives $Z$ and the marginals in $O(TK^2)$.
-   Its log-likelihood is concave, with gradient “observed minus expected features” (Theorem 4.4).
-   Taggers are scored by exact-match span F1, which is much stricter than token accuracy.
:::

## 5. Word embeddings {#ch5}

One-hot vectors make all words equally different. Embeddings place words in $\mathbb{R}^d$ so that words used in similar contexts are close: “you shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth, 1957). This chapter builds them from counts, then shows that word2vec factorises the same counts.

### 5.1 Counting contexts

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Co-occurrence counts and PMI]{.tag} Let $c(w, u)$ count how often the context word $u$ appears within a fixed window around the word $w$, typically 2 to 10 tokens on each side. Write $c(w)$ and $c(u)$ for the marginal counts and $D$ for the total. The pointwise mutual information and its positive part are
$$
\mathrm{PMI}(w, u) = \log \frac{c(w, u)\, D}{c(w)\, c(u)}, \qquad \mathrm{PPMI}(w, u) = \max(\mathrm{PMI}(w, u), 0) .
$$

PMI compares observed co-occurrence with independence; it discounts frequent words such as “the”.
:::

### 5.2 Low-rank factorisation

::: def
[Definition 5.2 — Embeddings by truncated SVD]{.tag} Write the singular value decomposition of the PPMI matrix as $M = U \Sigma V^\top$. The $d$-dimensional embedding of word $w$ is row $w$ of $U_d \Sigma_d^{1/2}$, and similarity is measured by the cosine
$$
\cos(a, b) = \frac{a^\top b}{\|a\|\, \|b\|} .
$$
:::

By the Eckart–Young theorem, $U_d \Sigma_d V_d^\top$ is the best rank-$d$ approximation of $M$ in Frobenius norm: it keeps the dominant structure of the counts and averages away noise.

::: ex
[Code 5.3 — PPMI and SVD on a synthetic corpus]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
groups = {"animal": ["cat", "dog", "horse", "cow"], "food": ["bread", "apple", "rice", "cheese"],
          "vehicle": ["car", "bus", "truck", "bike"], "place": ["road", "street", "bridge", "lane"]}
templates = [["the", "animal", "eats", "the", "food"], ["a", "animal", "sleeps"],
             ["food", "is", "tasty"], ["the", "vehicle", "drives", "on", "the", "place"],
             ["a", "vehicle", "is", "fast"], ["the", "place", "is", "wide"]]
corpus = []
for _ in range(4000):                                    # sample sentences from templates
    tpl = templates[rng.integers(len(templates))]
    corpus += [groups[w][rng.integers(4)] if w in groups else w for w in tpl] + ["."]
vocab = sorted(set(corpus)); idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
C = np.zeros((len(vocab), len(vocab)))
for i, w in enumerate(corpus):                           # symmetric window of 2 words
    for j in range(max(0, i - 2), min(len(corpus), i + 3)):
        if j != i:
            C[idx[w], idx[corpus[j]]] += 1
pmi = np.log(C * C.sum() / (C.sum(1, keepdims=True) * C.sum(0, keepdims=True)) + 1e-12)
ppmi = np.maximum(pmi, 0)                                # positive PMI
U, S, _ = np.linalg.svd(ppmi)
emb = U[:, :8] * np.sqrt(S[:8])                          # 8-dimensional word vectors
emb /= np.linalg.norm(emb, axis=1, keepdims=True)
for w in ["cat", "bread", "car", "road"]:
    sims = emb @ emb[idx[w]]
    print(f"{w:6s}->", [vocab[k] for k in np.argsort(-sims) if vocab[k] != w][:3])
```

The nearest neighbours of “cat” are the other animals, those of “bread” the other foods, and likewise for vehicles and places. Two animals almost never appear within two words of each other: they are close because they share contexts.
:::

### 5.3 Skip-gram with negative sampling

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS)]{.tag} word2vec (Mikolov and coauthors, 2013) gives each word a vector $\mathbf{w}$ and each context a vector $\mathbf{u}$. For each observed pair $(w, u)$ it draws $k$ negative contexts $u_1', \dots, u_k'$ from the unigram law $P_n$ and maximises
$$
\log \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{u}) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \log \sigma(-\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{u}_i'), \qquad \sigma(s) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-s}} .
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — SGNS factorises a shifted PMI matrix (Levy and Goldberg, 2014)]{.tag} If the dimension is large enough for each inner product to be set freely, and $P_n(u) = c(u)/D$, the SGNS objective summed over the corpus is maximised when
$$
\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{u} = \mathrm{PMI}(w, u) - \log k \quad \text{for every pair with } c(w, u) > 0 .
$$

::: proof
Summed over the corpus, the expected objective is a sum of independent terms, one per pair, in the variable $s = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{u}$:
$$
\ell(s) = c(w, u) \log \sigma(s) + k \frac{c(w)\, c(u)}{D} \log \sigma(-s) .
$$

Using $\sigma'(s) = \sigma(s)\sigma(-s)$, the derivative is $c(w, u)\, \sigma(-s) - k\, c(w) c(u) D^{-1}\, \sigma(s)$. It vanishes when
$$
e^{s} = \frac{\sigma(s)}{\sigma(-s)} = \frac{c(w, u)\, D}{k\, c(w)\, c(u)},
$$
that is $s = \mathrm{PMI}(w, u) - \log k$. Each $\ell$ is strictly concave, so this is the maximum. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Code 5.6 — Checking Theorem 5.5 numerically (continues Code 5.3)]{.tag}

```python
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(1); torch.manual_seed(0)
Ct = torch.tensor(C, dtype=torch.float32)
D = Ct.sum(); k = 5                                     # k negative samples per positive pair
neg = k * Ct.sum(1, keepdim=True) * Ct.sum(0, keepdim=True) / D   # expected negatives
V, d = C.shape[0], C.shape[0]                           # full rank: d = |V|
Wv = (0.1 * torch.randn(V, d)).requires_grad_(); Cv = (0.1 * torch.randn(V, d)).requires_grad_()
opt = torch.optim.Adam([Wv, Cv], lr=0.05)
for step in range(3000):                                # SGNS objective summed over the corpus
    s = Wv @ Cv.T
    loss = -(Ct * torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(s) + neg * torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(-s)).sum() / D
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
s = (Wv @ Cv.T).detach().numpy()
mask = C >= 20                                          # pairs seen at least 20 times
gap = np.abs(s - (pmi - np.log(k)))[mask].max()
print("pairs:", mask.sum(), " max |w.u - (PMI - log k)| =", gap.round(3))
```

On the 263 pairs seen at least 20 times, the learned inner products match $\mathrm{PMI} - \log 5$ within 0.002.
:::

word2vec, GloVe and PPMI–SVD thus factorise the same statistics. GloVe (Pennington, Socher and Manning, 2014) fits $\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{u} + b_w + b_u \approx \log c(w, u)$ by weighted least squares. fastText (Bojanowski and coauthors, 2017) sums the vectors of a word's character n-grams, so it embeds unseen words.

### 5.4 Analogies, limits and bias

Differences of vectors encode some relations (Mikolov, Yih and Zweig, 2013). The nearest word to
$$
\mathbf{w}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{w}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{w}_{\text{woman}}
$$
is often “queen”, once the three query words are excluded. The same arithmetic reproduces stereotypes of the training text, for instance between gender and occupations (Bolukbasi and coauthors, 2016). A static embedding also gives one vector per type, whatever its sense; contextual representations (ch. 7) fix this.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Words are represented by their contexts; PPMI reweights co-occurrence counts.
-   A truncated SVD gives the best low-rank summary of the PPMI matrix.
-   SGNS implicitly factorises the PMI matrix shifted by $\log k$ (Theorem 5.5).
-   Embeddings support analogies but inherit the biases of their corpus, and give one vector per type.
:::

## 6. Deep learning for NLP: recurrent networks, attention and transformers {#ch6}

An n-gram model forgets everything beyond a few tokens; neural sequence models keep a learned summary of the prefix. This chapter presents the two answers, recurrence and attention, and why the second won.

### 6.1 Recurrent networks and their gradients

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Recurrent neural network (RNN)]{.tag} Given input vectors $x_1, \dots, x_T$ (embeddings, ch. 5), an Elman RNN updates a hidden state
$$
h_t = \tanh(W h_{t-1} + U x_t + b),
$$
and predicts from $h_t$, for example the next token by $\mathrm{softmax}(V h_t)$. Backpropagation through time differentiates the network unrolled over the sequence, a deep network with shared weights.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Vanishing gradients]{.tag} For $t < T$, in operator norm,
$$
\Big\| \frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_t} \Big\| \leq \|W\|^{T - t} .
$$

If $\|W\| < 1$, the influence of $h_t$ on time $T$ decays exponentially with the distance.

::: proof
The chain rule gives a product of Jacobians:
$$
\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_t} = \prod_{s = t+1}^{T} \mathrm{diag}\big(1 - h_s^2\big)\, W .
$$

Each diagonal factor has norm at most 1 because $|\tanh'| \leq 1$, and the operator norm is sub-multiplicative. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

When $\|W\| > 1$ the product can explode instead, and gradients are clipped (Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio, 2013).

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — Long short-term memory (LSTM)]{.tag} An LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) adds a memory cell $c_t$ controlled by three gates: forget $f_t$, input $i_t$ and output $o_t$. Each gate is a sigmoid of an affine function of the previous state and the current input, with values in $(0, 1)$, and
$$
c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tanh(W_c h_{t-1} + U_c x_t + b_c), \qquad h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) .
$$
:::

Along the direct path through the cell, the Jacobian $\partial c_t / \partial c_{t-1}$ is $\mathrm{diag}(f_t)$, with no weight matrix: when $f_t$ stays close to 1, the error signal crosses many steps intact.

### 6.2 Attention

An encoder–decoder encodes the source into states $h_1, \dots, h_S$ and decodes the target token by token. A single vector cannot hold a long sentence; attention lets each decoding step look at all source states (Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio, 2015).

::: def
[Definition 6.4 — Attention as a soft lookup]{.tag} For a query $q$, keys $k_s$ and values $v_s$, attention returns
$$
\mathrm{att}(q) = \sum_{s=1}^{S} a_s v_s, \qquad a = \mathrm{softmax}\big(\mathrm{score}(q, k_1), \dots, \mathrm{score}(q, k_S)\big) .
$$

The output is a convex combination of the values.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Scaled dot-product attention]{.tag} Stack $T$ queries, keys and values in matrices $Q, K \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}$ and $V$. Then
$$
\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\Big( \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d}} \Big) V,
$$
with the softmax applied row by row. In *self*-attention, the three matrices are linear maps of the same sequence $X$:
$$
Q = X W_Q, \qquad K = X W_K, \qquad V = X W_V .
$$

A *causal* mask sets the scores of future positions to $-\infty$, so that position $t$ only sees positions up to $t$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.6 — Why divide by $\sqrt{d}$]{.tag} If $q, k \in \mathbb{R}^d$ have independent entries of mean 0 and variance 1, then
$$
\mathbb{E}[q^\top k] = 0, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(q^\top k) = d .
$$

::: proof
$q^\top k = \sum_{i=1}^d q_i k_i$ is a sum of $d$ independent terms. Each has mean $\mathbb{E}[q_i]\mathbb{E}[k_i] = 0$ and variance $\mathbb{E}[q_i^2]\mathbb{E}[k_i^2] = 1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Unscaled scores of standard deviation $\sqrt{d}$, 16 for $d = 256$, saturate the softmax into a near one-hot vector with vanishing gradient; dividing by $\sqrt{d}$ restores variance 1.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.7 — Self-attention ignores order]{.tag} Without a mask and without positional information, self-attention is permutation-equivariant: for every permutation matrix $P$,
$$
\mathrm{Attention}(PX W_Q, PX W_K, PX W_V) = P\, \mathrm{Attention}(XW_Q, XW_K, XW_V) .
$$

::: proof
The scores become $P Q K^\top P^\top$; a row-wise softmax commutes with both permutations, and $P^\top P = I$ cancels against $PV$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Order must be injected: the original transformer adds sinusoidal position vectors to the embeddings; rotary embeddings rotate queries and keys by angles proportional to the position (Su and coauthors, 2021).

### 6.3 The transformer block

::: def
[Definition 6.8 — Transformer block]{.tag} A block maps $H \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}$ to a matrix of the same shape, with layer normalisation (LN) before each sub-layer:
$$
H' = H + \mathrm{MHA}(\mathrm{LN}(H)), \qquad H'' = H' + \mathrm{FFN}(\mathrm{LN}(H')) .
$$

Multi-head attention (MHA) runs $h$ attentions of dimension $d / h$ in parallel and concatenates them; the feed-forward network (FFN) is a two-layer perceptron of width about $4d$ at each position. Vaswani and coauthors (2017) placed LN after each residual sum; the pre-LN form above is now standard.
:::

A layer costs $O(T^2 d + T d^2)$ but processes all positions in parallel, where an RNN needs $T$ sequential steps; this made training on billions of tokens possible (ch. 7).

::: ex
[Code 6.9 — Causality, equivariance and scaling]{.tag}

```python
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(1); torch.manual_seed(0)

def attention(Q, K, V, causal=False):
    """Scaled dot-product attention softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V, optionally causal."""
    S = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / K.shape[-1] ** 0.5
    if causal:
        T = S.shape[-1]
        S = S.masked_fill(torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), 1), float("-inf"))
    return torch.softmax(S, dim=-1) @ V

T, d = 6, 64
X = torch.randn(T, d)
Wq, Wk, Wv = (torch.randn(d, d) / d ** 0.5 for _ in range(3))
Y = attention(X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv, causal=True)
X2 = X.clone(); X2[4:] = torch.randn(2, d)              # change the last two tokens
Y2 = attention(X2 @ Wq, X2 @ Wk, X2 @ Wv, causal=True)
print("causal: outputs 0-3 unchanged:", torch.allclose(Y[:4], Y2[:4]), "| output 4 changed:", not torch.allclose(Y[4], Y2[4]))
P = torch.randperm(T)                                   # no positions: permutation equivariance
Z, Zp = attention(X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv), attention(X[P] @ Wq, X[P] @ Wk, X[P] @ Wv)
print("equivariant:", torch.allclose(Z[P], Zp, atol=1e-6))
for dk in [16, 256]:                                    # why divide by sqrt(d)
    q, k = torch.randn(10000, dk), torch.randn(10000, dk)
    print(f"d = {dk:3d}: var(q.k) = {(q * k).sum(1).var():.1f}, after scaling = {((q * k).sum(1) / dk ** 0.5).var():.2f}")
```

Changing tokens 5 and 6 leaves the first four causal outputs unchanged; permuting inputs permutes outputs; the variances of $q^\top k$ are 15.5 and 255.5 before scaling, 0.97 and 1.00 after.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   RNN gradients are products of Jacobians and vanish or explode exponentially with distance (Proposition 6.2).
-   The LSTM cell provides an additive path whose Jacobian is the forget gate.
-   Attention is a differentiable soft lookup; scaling by $1/\sqrt{d}$ keeps the scores of order 1.
-   Self-attention is blind to order without positions; transformers trade $O(T^2)$ cost for parallelism.
:::

## 7. Neural language modelling and large language models {#ch7}

Predicting the next token well requires syntax, facts and some reasoning. This chapter replaces count tables by neural networks, states the limit no model can beat, and follows the path from pretraining to an assistant.

### 7.1 Neural language models

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Neural language model]{.tag} A neural LM computes $P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}) = \mathrm{softmax}(V h_t)$ from a learned summary $h_t$ of the prefix, trained by minimising the cross-entropy. For Bengio and coauthors (2003), $h_t$ is a perceptron on the embeddings of the $n - 1$ previous tokens; in an RNN LM it is the recurrent state; in a transformer LM, the output of causal self-attention (ch. 6).
:::

Shared embeddings generalise: having seen “the cat sat”, the model favours “the dog sat”, since the two animals have close vectors.

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — No model beats the source]{.tag} Let the text be drawn from a source $p$. For every model $q$ and every position $t$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[-\log q(w_t \mid w_{<t})\big] \geq \mathbb{E}\big[-\log p(w_t \mid w_{<t})\big] ,
$$
so the expected log-perplexity of any model is at least the conditional entropy of the source.

::: proof
Given the prefix, the expectation over $w_t$ is a cross-entropy between the two conditional laws, at least the entropy of the first (Proposition 0.2). Average over the prefix. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Code 7.3 — A neural n-gram model against the entropy of its source]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(1); torch.manual_seed(0); rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
V, N = 8, 30000                                          # a source of order 2 over 8 symbols
P = rng.dirichlet(0.3 * np.ones(V), size=(V, V))         # P[a, b] = law of x_t given (a, b)
u = rng.random(N); x = [0, 1]
for t in range(N):                                       # inverse-CDF sampling
    x.append(min(int(np.searchsorted(P[x[-2], x[-1]].cumsum(), u[t])), V - 1))
x = torch.tensor(x)
train, test = x[:25000], x[25000:]
true_nll = -np.log(P[test[:-2], test[1:-1], test[2:]]).mean()
print(f"true source: test perplexity {np.exp(true_nll):.3f}")

class MLPLM(torch.nn.Module):                            # Bengio-style neural n-gram model
    def __init__(self, n, d=16, h=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.emb = torch.nn.Embedding(V, d)
        self.mlp = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(n * d, h), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(h, V))
    def forward(self, ctx):                              # ctx: (batch, n) previous symbols
        return self.mlp(self.emb(ctx).flatten(1))

for n in [1, 2]:
    model = MLPLM(n); opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    windows = lambda s: torch.stack([s[i: len(s) - n + i] for i in range(n)], 1)
    for epoch in range(200):                             # full-batch training
        loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(windows(train)), train[n:])
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        ce = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(windows(test)), test[n:])
    print(f"context of {n} symbol(s): test perplexity {ce.exp():.3f}")
```

The true source has test perplexity 3.666. A model that sees one symbol is stuck at 7.164; with two, the true order, it reaches 3.692, just above the bound of Proposition 7.2.
:::

### 7.2 Pretraining

::: def
[Definition 7.4 — Pretraining objectives]{.tag}

-   **Causal LM** (GPT series): predict each token from its prefix; the model generates text.
-   **Masked LM** (BERT, Devlin and coauthors, 2019): replace 15 % of the tokens by a mask (80 % of the time), a random token (10 %) or themselves (10 %), and predict the originals from both sides; the model encodes text for classification and tagging.
-   **Denoising** (T5, Raffel and coauthors, 2020): corrupt input spans and regenerate them with an encoder–decoder.
:::

The resulting vectors are contextual: “bank” differs in “river bank” and “bank loan”, unlike in ch. 5.

::: def
[Definition 7.5 — Scaling law]{.tag} Hoffmann and coauthors (2022) fit the final loss of a model with $N$ parameters trained on $D$ tokens as
$$
L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}},
$$
and training costs about $C \approx 6 N D$ floating-point operations.
:::

Under a budget $C$, the optimal $N$ and $D$ grow as powers of $C$ with similar exponents (Exercise 16), about 20 tokens per parameter: Chinchilla (70 billion parameters, 1.4 trillion tokens) beat larger models trained on less data.

### 7.3 Decoding

::: def
[Definition 7.6 — Sampling with temperature, top-k and nucleus]{.tag} Given next-token logits $z$:

-   *greedy* decoding takes $\arg\max_k z_k$;
-   *temperature* sampling draws from $\mathrm{softmax}(z / T)$ (Definition 0.3); $T < 1$ sharpens the law, $T > 1$ flattens it;
-   *top-k* sampling keeps the $k$ most probable tokens and renormalises;
-   *nucleus* (top-p) sampling keeps the smallest set of most probable tokens whose mass reaches $p$, and renormalises (Holtzman and coauthors, 2020).
:::

Greedy and beam search (ch. 8) give bland, repetitive open-ended text; nucleus sampling adapts the number of candidates to the model's confidence.

::: ex
[Code 7.7 — Temperature and nucleus size]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
logits = np.array([3.0, 2.5, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.0, -1.0, -2.0])   # scores of 8 next tokens

def softmax(z, T=1.0):
    e = np.exp((z - z.max()) / T); return e / e.sum()

def nucleus(p, top_p=0.9):
    """Smallest set of most probable tokens whose mass reaches top_p, renormalised."""
    order = np.argsort(-p)
    keep = order[: np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(p[order]), top_p) + 1]
    q = np.zeros_like(p); q[keep] = p[keep]
    return q / q.sum()

for T in [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]:
    p = softmax(logits, T)
    H = -(p * np.log(p)).sum()
    print(f"T = {T}: entropy {H:.2f} nats, top-0.9 nucleus keeps {np.count_nonzero(nucleus(p))} tokens")
print("one nucleus sample at T = 1:", rng.choice(8, p=nucleus(softmax(logits))))
```

From $T = 0.5$ to 1 to 2, the entropy grows from 0.92 to 1.44 to 1.83 nats, and the 0.9-nucleus from 3 to 4 to 6 tokens.
:::

### 7.4 From a language model to an assistant

A pretrained model continues text; an assistant follows instructions. Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations comes first. Then reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF, Ouyang and coauthors, 2022) fits a reward model to human comparisons of answers and maximises it while staying close to the fine-tuned model; DPO (Rafailov and coauthors, 2023) reaches the same optimum by a logistic loss on the pairs ([ch. 13](#ch13), 13.4).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 7

-   Neural LMs generalise through embeddings; the source entropy bounds their perplexity (Proposition 7.2).
-   Causal, masked and denoising objectives give generators, encoders and encoder–decoders.
-   Under a compute budget $C \approx 6ND$, parameters and data should grow together.
-   Decoding is a design choice: temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling trade diversity for reliability.
-   Assistants add instruction tuning and preference optimisation (RLHF, DPO) to pretraining.
:::

## 8. Machine translation {#ch8}

Translation was the first application of the field and remains its benchmark. This chapter follows its three paradigms, rules, alignment models learned by EM and neural encoder–decoders, then the metrics that decided between them.

### 8.1 From rules to statistics

Rule-based systems, from the 1954 Georgetown–IBM demonstration on, combined bilingual dictionaries with hand-written transfer rules. Statistical translation (Brown and coauthors, 1993) learned from parallel text, with the noisy channel $\hat e = \arg\max_e P(f \mid e) P(e)$ for a foreign sentence $f$. Phrase-based systems (Koehn, Och and Marcu, 2003) dominated until about 2016.

### 8.2 Word alignment with IBM Model 1

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — IBM Model 1]{.tag} Let $e = e_1 \dots e_m$ be a sentence and $f = f_0 f_1 \dots f_l$ its source, where $f_0$ is a NULL word. Each target word $e_j$ is aligned to one source position $a_j$, chosen uniformly, and then drawn from a translation table $t(e_j \mid f_{a_j})$:
$$
P(e, a \mid f) = \frac{\varepsilon}{(l + 1)^m} \prod_{j=1}^{m} t(e_j \mid f_{a_j}) .
$$

In the noisy channel of 8.1, the roles of $e$ and $f$ are exchanged.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 8.2 — Likelihood and EM for Model 1]{.tag} Summing over the $(l + 1)^m$ alignments gives a product of sums:
$$
P(e \mid f) = \frac{\varepsilon}{(l + 1)^m} \prod_{j=1}^{m} \sum_{i=0}^{l} t(e_j \mid f_i) .
$$

The alignment posterior factorises over target positions, $P(a_j = i \mid e, f) \propto t(e_j \mid f_i)$, and EM updates $t(e \mid f)$ to the expected count of the pair $(e, f)$, divided by the expected count of $f$.

::: proof
The sum over $a = (a_1, \dots, a_m)$ of a product whose $j$-th factor depends only on $a_j$ is the product of the sums (distributivity), and the posterior factorises likewise. The M-step is Proposition 1.5 with fractional counts. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The log-likelihood, a sum of logarithms of linear functions of $t$, is concave: every local maximum is global.

::: ex
[Code 8.3 — EM on three sentence pairs (no NULL word)]{.tag}

```python
from collections import defaultdict

pairs = [("das Haus", "the house"), ("das Buch", "the book"), ("ein Buch", "a book")]
pairs = [(f.split(), e.split()) for f, e in pairs]
E = {e for _, es in pairs for e in es}
t = defaultdict(lambda: 1.0 / len(E))                   # t[e, f] = P(e | f), uniform start
for it in range(1, 21):                                 # EM for IBM Model 1
    count, total = defaultdict(float), defaultdict(float)
    for fs, es in pairs:
        for e in es:
            z = sum(t[e, f] for f in fs)                # E-step: P(a_j = i | e, f)
            for f in fs:
                count[e, f] += t[e, f] / z; total[f] += t[e, f] / z
    for (e, f) in count:                                # M-step: renormalise expected counts
        t[e, f] = count[e, f] / total[f]
    if it in (1, 2, 5, 20):
        print(f"iteration {it:2d}: t(house|Haus) = {t['house', 'Haus']:.3f}, "
              f"t(the|das) = {t['the', 'das']:.3f}, t(book|ein) = {t['book', 'ein']:.3f}")
```

After one iteration the three printed entries are 0.5. After 20, $t(\text{house} \mid \text{Haus}) = 0.968$, $t(\text{the} \mid \text{das}) = 1.000$, and $t(\text{book} \mid \text{ein})$ has fallen to 0.032: “Buch” explains “book”, which frees “ein” to explain “a”.
:::

### 8.3 Neural machine translation

A neural system is an attention encoder–decoder (ch. 6) trained to maximise $\sum_j \log P_\theta(e_j \mid e_{<j}, f)$, with the reference prefix fed to the decoder (teacher forcing). Subwords (ch. 1) handle rare words; back-translating monolingual target text adds synthetic pairs (Sennrich, Haddow and Birch, 2016b).

::: def
[Definition 8.4 — Beam search]{.tag} Keep the $B$ best partial translations; at each step, extend each by every token, score by total log-probability, keep the best $B$, and set aside those ending with `</s>`. Return the finished hypothesis with the best score divided by its length to a power $\lambda$, since raw log-probabilities favour short outputs.
:::

### 8.4 Evaluation

::: def
[Definition 8.5 — BLEU (Papineni and coauthors, 2002)]{.tag} Let $p_n$ be the corpus-level precision of the hypothesis n-grams, where each n-gram is counted at most as many times as it appears in the reference (clipping). Let $h$ and $r$ be the total hypothesis and reference lengths. Then
$$
\mathrm{BLEU} = \mathrm{BP} \cdot \exp\Big( \frac{1}{4} \sum_{n=1}^{4} \log p_n \Big), \qquad \mathrm{BP} = \min\big(1, e^{1 - r/h}\big) .
$$
:::

::: ex
[Code 8.6 — BLEU with clipping and brevity penalty]{.tag}

```python
import math
from collections import Counter

def ngrams(words, n):
    return Counter(tuple(words[i: i + n]) for i in range(len(words) - n + 1))

def bleu(hyps, refs, N=4):
    """Corpus BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002): clipped n-gram precisions, brevity penalty."""
    match, total, h_len, r_len = [0] * N, [0] * N, 0, 0
    for h, r in zip(hyps, refs):
        h, r = h.split(), r.split()
        h_len += len(h); r_len += len(r)
        for n in range(1, N + 1):
            hn, rn = ngrams(h, n), ngrams(r, n)
            match[n - 1] += sum(min(c, rn[g]) for g, c in hn.items())   # clipping
            total[n - 1] += max(len(h) - n + 1, 0)
    prec = [m / t for m, t in zip(match, total)]
    bp = 1.0 if h_len > r_len else math.exp(1 - r_len / h_len)
    score = bp * math.exp(sum(math.log(p) for p in prec) / N) if min(prec) > 0 else 0.0
    return score, prec, bp

print(bleu(["the the the the the the the"], ["the cat is on the mat"], N=1))
refs = ["the cat is on the mat", "there is a book on the table"]
hyps = ["the cat sat on the mat", "there is a book on a table"]
score, prec, bp = bleu(hyps, refs)
print("BLEU =", round(100 * score, 1), " precisions", [round(p, 3) for p in prec], " BP", round(bp, 3))
```

Clipping limits “the the the …” to a unigram precision of 2/7. The two-sentence corpus has precisions 11/13, 7/11, 4/9 and 2/7, no brevity penalty, and
$$
\mathrm{BLEU} = 100 \cdot \Big( \frac{11}{13} \cdot \frac{7}{11} \cdot \frac{4}{9} \cdot \frac{2}{7} \Big)^{1/4} = 100 \cdot \Big( \frac{8}{117} \Big)^{1/4} \approx 51.1 .
$$
:::

BLEU rewards surface overlap: it misses paraphrases and depends on tokenisation, hence fixed tools such as sacreBLEU (Post, 2018). chrF compares character n-grams; COMET (Rei and coauthors, 2020) is a network trained to predict human judgements, and agrees better with them.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 8

-   IBM Model 1 explains a sentence pair by hidden word alignments; distributivity makes its likelihood a product of sums.
-   EM on Model 1 is a concave problem; it discovers translation pairs from co-occurrence alone.
-   Neural MT is an attention encoder–decoder decoded by beam search with length normalisation.
-   BLEU is a clipped n-gram precision with a brevity penalty; learned metrics such as COMET track human judgements better.
:::

## 9. Sentiment analysis {#ch9}

Is this review positive? Is the customer annoyed with the battery or the screen? This chapter defines the sentiment tasks, shows that the classic baseline is a linear model, and locates where it breaks: negation and composition.

### 9.1 Tasks

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Sentiment tasks]{.tag}

-   *Polarity classification*: assign a document or sentence to positive or negative, sometimes with a neutral class.
-   *Rating prediction*: predict a score, such as 1 to 5 stars, by ordinal regression.
-   *Aspect-based analysis*: extract opinions as tuples (target entity, aspect, polarity, holder, time) (Liu, 2012); in “great screen, awful battery” the two aspects have opposite polarities.
:::

Benchmarks include movie reviews (Pang, Lee and Vaithyanathan, 2002) and the Stanford Sentiment Treebank, labelled on every phrase of a parse tree (Socher and coauthors, 2013).

### 9.2 Linear baselines

::: def
[Definition 9.2 — Multinomial naive Bayes]{.tag} A document is a bag of words with counts $n_w$. Naive Bayes assumes the words independent given the class $y$:
$$
P(y \mid x) \propto P(y) \prod_{w} \theta_{y w}^{\, n_w},
$$
with $\theta_{yw}$ estimated by add-one smoothed relative frequencies within class $y$ (Definition 1.7).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 9.3 — Naive Bayes is a linear classifier]{.tag} For two classes, the log-odds are affine in the counts:
$$
\log \frac{P(+ \mid x)}{P(- \mid x)} = \log \frac{P(+)}{P(-)} + \sum_{w} n_w \log \frac{\theta_{+w}}{\theta_{-w}} .
$$

::: proof
Take the logarithm of the ratio of the two expressions of Definition 9.2; the normalising constant cancels. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Logistic regression fits the same linear form discriminatively. Both give each word a fixed weight, whatever its neighbours: exactly what negation violates.

::: ex
[Code 9.4 — Negation defeats bags of words]{.tag}

```python
import re
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pos, neg = ["good", "great", "excellent", "fun"], ["bad", "boring", "awful", "dull"]
subj, filler = ["the film", "the plot", "the acting", "this movie"], ["really", "quite", "honestly", ""]
docs, y = [], []
for _ in range(2000):                                   # synthetic reviews with negation
    label, negated = rng.integers(2), rng.random() < 0.4
    adj = (pos if label != negated else neg)[rng.integers(4)]
    docs.append(f"{subj[rng.integers(4)]} was {'not ' if negated else ''}{filler[rng.integers(4)]} {adj}")
    y.append(int(label))
y = np.array(y)
y_noisy = np.where(rng.random(len(y)) < 0.05, 1 - y, y)  # 5 % annotation noise

def mark_negation(s):
    """Prefix NOT_ to every word after 'not', as in Pang et al. (2002)."""
    return re.sub(r"\bnot\s+(.*)$", lambda m: " ".join("NOT_" + w for w in m.group(1).split()), s)

tr, te = slice(0, 1500), slice(1500, 2000)
for name, prep, ngram in [("unigrams", None, (1, 1)), ("uni+bigrams", None, (1, 2)),
                          ("NOT_ marking", mark_negation, (1, 1))]:
    vec = CountVectorizer(preprocessor=prep, ngram_range=ngram, token_pattern=r"\S+")
    Xtr, Xte = vec.fit_transform(docs[tr]), vec.transform(docs[te])
    accs = [m.fit(Xtr, y_noisy[tr]).score(Xte, y[te]) for m in (MultinomialNB(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]
    print(f"{name:13s} naive Bayes {accs[0]:.3f}   logistic regression {accs[1]:.3f}")
```

With unigrams both classifiers reach 56.4 % on clean test labels: “not” appears in both classes and cannot flip “good”. Bigrams reach only 68–69 %, as a filler word often separates “not” from the adjective. Marking the words after “not” gives 100 %.
:::

### 9.3 Composition and neural models

Real negation has a scope (“not only good but great”), and contrast and irony change polarity in ways no fixed list captures. Recursive networks over parse trees targeted this composition (Socher and coauthors, 2013); today a fine-tuned pretrained transformer (ch. 7) learns it from data. In dialogue, prosody and the partner's turns matter too ([ch. 14](#ch14)).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 9

-   Sentiment tasks range from document polarity to aspect-level tuples.
-   Naive Bayes and logistic regression are linear in word counts (Proposition 9.3).
-   Negation and composition break bag-of-words models; marking the scope or using contextual models restores them.
-   Fine-tuned transformers learn composition from data; dialogue adds prosody and context.
:::

## 10. Speech recognition and speech synthesis {#ch10}

Ch. 3 recognised speech with HMMs, a lexicon and a grammar. Modern recognisers map frames to characters with one network trained end to end, and synthesisers run the other way. This chapter gives the loss that made end-to-end recognition possible, then the synthesis pipeline.

### 10.1 Measuring recognition

::: def
[Definition 10.1 — Word error rate (WER)]{.tag} Align hypothesis and reference with a minimal number of word substitutions $S$, deletions $D$ and insertions $I$ (a Levenshtein distance, by dynamic programming in the tropical semiring). With $N$ reference words,
$$
\mathrm{WER} = \frac{S + D + I}{N} .
$$

Insertions can push it above 100 %. The character error rate (CER) is the same on characters.
:::

::: ex
[Code 10.2 — WER with the error types]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np

def wer(ref, hyp):
    """Word error rate (S + D + I) / N from the Levenshtein alignment of word sequences."""
    r, h = ref.split(), hyp.split()
    D = np.zeros((len(r) + 1, len(h) + 1), dtype=int)
    D[:, 0], D[0, :] = np.arange(len(r) + 1), np.arange(len(h) + 1)
    for i in range(1, len(r) + 1):
        for j in range(1, len(h) + 1):
            D[i, j] = min(D[i - 1, j - 1] + (r[i - 1] != h[j - 1]), D[i - 1, j] + 1, D[i, j - 1] + 1)
    i, j, ops = len(r), len(h), {"S": 0, "D": 0, "I": 0}
```
