```python
    while i > 0 or j > 0:                                 # backtrace to count error types
        if i > 0 and j > 0 and D[i, j] == D[i - 1, j - 1] + (r[i - 1] != h[j - 1]):
            ops["S"] += r[i - 1] != h[j - 1]; i, j = i - 1, j - 1
        elif i > 0 and D[i, j] == D[i - 1, j] + 1:
            ops["D"] += 1; i -= 1
        else:
            ops["I"] += 1; j -= 1
    return round(D[-1, -1] / len(r), 3), ops

print(*wer("i want to recognise speech today", "i want to wreck a nice beach today"))
print(*wer("the cat sat", "the cat sat down on the mat"))   # insertions only: WER above 100 %
```

“recognise speech” heard as “wreck a nice beach” costs 2 substitutions and 2 insertions on 6 words: WER 0.667. Four insertions on three words give 1.333.
:::

### 10.2 Connectionist temporal classification

Nobody annotates which frame belongs to which character; CTC (Graves and coauthors, 2006) sums over all alignments.

::: def
[Definition 10.3 — CTC]{.tag} A network outputs, at each of $T$ frames, a law $y_t$ over the alphabet plus a *blank* symbol $\varnothing$. A path $\pi$ chooses one symbol per frame and has probability $\prod_t y_t(\pi_t)$.

The collapse map $\mathcal{B}$ merges repeated symbols, then deletes blanks: for example $\mathcal{B}(aa\varnothing ab) = aab$. The CTC likelihood of a label sequence $l$ is
$$
P(l \mid x) = \sum_{\pi \,:\, \mathcal{B}(\pi) = l} \ \prod_{t=1}^{T} y_t(\pi_t),
$$
and the loss is $-\log P(l \mid x)$. Repeated labels need a blank between them.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 10.4 — CTC forward recursion]{.tag} Insert blanks at the start, at the end and between the labels, to get an extended sequence $l'$ of length $S = 2|l| + 1$. Let $\alpha_t(s)$ be the total probability of the path prefixes of length $t$ that run through $l'_1, \dots, l'_s$ in order, possibly skipping blanks, and end on $l'_s$. The prefixes of length 1 give
$$
\alpha_1(1) = y_1(\varnothing), \qquad \alpha_1(2) = y_1(l_1),
$$
and for $t \geq 2$
$$
\alpha_t(s) = \Big( \alpha_{t-1}(s) + \alpha_{t-1}(s-1) + \mathbf{1}[l'_s \neq \varnothing,\ l'_s \neq l'_{s-2}]\ \alpha_{t-1}(s-2) \Big)\, y_t(l'_s),
$$
with $P(l \mid x) = \alpha_T(S) + \alpha_T(S - 1)$, in $O(T |l|)$ operations.

::: proof
A valid path visits the symbols of $l'$ in order, staying on a symbol for one or more frames. To be at position $s$ at time $t$, it was one frame earlier either already on $s$, or on the previous position, or two positions back when it skips the blank in between.

The skip is allowed only if $l'_s$ is a label different from $l'_{s-2}$: skipping the blank between equal labels would merge them under $\mathcal{B}$. The three cases partition the prefixes, with the common factor $y_t(l'_s)$ (Proposition 0.6). A complete path ends on the last label or the final blank. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Code 10.5 — The recursion against brute force and PyTorch]{.tag}

```python
import itertools
import torch
torch.set_num_threads(1); torch.manual_seed(0)
T, C = 6, 4                                              # 6 frames; symbols: blank=0, a=1, b=2, c=3
logp = torch.randn(T, C).log_softmax(-1)                 # frame-wise log-probabilities
y = [1, 2, 2]                                            # target "a b b" (repeated b needs a blank)

def ctc_forward(logp, y, blank=0):
    """CTC forward algorithm on the extended label sequence  _ y1 _ y2 _ ... _ yU _."""
    z = [blank]
    for s in y:
        z += [s, blank]
    S = len(z)
    alpha = torch.full((S,), float("-inf"))
    alpha[0], alpha[1] = logp[0, z[0]], logp[0, z[1]]
    for t in range(1, len(logp)):
        prev = alpha.clone()
        for s in range(S):
            cands = [prev[s]] + ([prev[s - 1]] if s >= 1 else [])
            if s >= 2 and z[s] != blank and z[s] != z[s - 2]:
                cands.append(prev[s - 2])                # skip a blank between different labels
            alpha[s] = torch.logsumexp(torch.stack(cands), 0) + logp[t, z[s]]
    return -torch.logsumexp(alpha[-2:], 0)               # end on the last label or final blank

def collapse(path, blank=0):
    out = [k for i, k in enumerate(path) if i == 0 or k != path[i - 1]]
    return [k for k in out if k != blank]

brute = -torch.logsumexp(torch.stack([logp[range(T), list(p)].sum() for p in
                         itertools.product(range(C), repeat=T) if collapse(list(p)) == y]), 0)
ref = torch.nn.functional.ctc_loss(logp[:, None], torch.tensor([y]), [T], [len(y)], reduction="sum")
print(f"forward {ctc_forward(logp, y):.4f}   brute force over 4^6 paths {brute:.4f}   torch {ref:.4f}")
```

The three computations of $-\log P(abb \mid x)$ agree: 4.4706.
:::

CTC assumes frame outputs independent given the input; it is decoded greedily (best symbol per frame, then $\mathcal{B}$) or with a beam and an LM. Attention encoder–decoders (Chan and coauthors, 2016) and the RNN transducer ([ch. 13](#ch13), 13.3) drop this assumption.

### 10.3 Self-supervised and weakly supervised speech

wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski and coauthors, 2020) masks latent frames computed from the waveform and learns, contrastively, to identify the quantised latent of each; fine-tuned with CTC, it works with ten minutes of transcribed audio. HuBERT (Hsu and coauthors, 2021) predicts k-means labels of masked frames. Whisper (Radford and coauthors, 2023) trains an encoder–decoder on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised audio.

### 10.4 Speech synthesis

Text-to-speech runs four stages: text normalisation (“Dr.” to “doctor”), grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, an acoustic model with durations and pitch, and a vocoder producing the waveform. Neural systems replaced concatenation of recorded units and HMM-based synthesis.

::: def
[Definition 10.6 — Neural synthesis components]{.tag}

-   *Acoustic model*: Tacotron 2 (Shen and coauthors, 2018) generates a mel spectrogram from characters with an attention encoder–decoder; FastSpeech 2 (Ren and coauthors, 2021) predicts durations, pitch and energy, and all frames in parallel.
-   *Vocoder*: WaveNet (van den Oord and coauthors, 2016) predicts each sample from the previous ones with dilated causal convolutions, over 256 classes from μ-law companding ($\mu = 255$):
    $$
    F(x) = \mathrm{sign}(x)\, \frac{\ln(1 + \mu |x|)}{\ln(1 + \mu)}, \qquad x \in [-1, 1] .
    $$
    HiFi-GAN (Kong, Kim and Bae, 2020), trained adversarially, generates all samples in parallel, much faster than real time.
:::

::: ex
[Example 10.7 — Why μ-law]{.tag} With $\mu = 255$, a quiet sample $x = 0.01$ maps to
$$
F(0.01) = \frac{\ln 3.55}{\ln 256} \approx 0.23 .
$$

Cut $[-1, 1]$ into 256 levels of width $2/255$. Amplitudes in $[0, 0.01]$ then get about 29 levels after companding, against 1.3 without. The loud range $[0.5, 1]$ gets 16 levels instead of 64: the levels go where speech samples mostly are, near zero.
:::

Listeners judge synthesis on a 1-to-5 scale, the mean opinion score (MOS), since no automatic metric captures naturalness well (ch. 12). Spoken language models without text are in [ch. 14](#ch14).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 10

-   WER is a normalised Levenshtein distance; insertions can push it above 100 %.
-   CTC sums over all monotonic alignments with blanks, by a forward recursion on the extended label sequence (Theorem 10.4).
-   Self-supervision (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT) and weak supervision (Whisper) cut the need for transcripts.
-   Synthesis runs text normalisation, phonemes, an acoustic model and a vocoder; it is judged by MOS.
:::

## 11. Chatbots, code generation and agents {#ch11}

A chatbot keeps a conversation going, a code generator writes programs that run, an agent acts over many steps. This chapter goes from pattern matching to LLM-based systems.

### 11.1 From ELIZA to task-oriented dialogue

ELIZA (Weizenbaum, 1966) matched keywords and rewrote the user's sentence (“I feel sad” gives “Why do you feel sad?”) with no model of meaning; users still confided in it. Task-oriented systems, which book a train or a table, are modular.

::: def
[Definition 11.1 — Task-oriented dialogue pipeline]{.tag}

-   *Understanding*: classify the intent and fill the slots, by sequence labelling (ch. 4): “a table for two at eight” gives `people=2, time=20:00`.
-   *State tracking*: update a belief over slot values from the history.
-   *Policy*: choose the next act (ask, confirm, query a database), possibly by reinforcement learning in a partially observable Markov decision process (Young and coauthors, 2013).
-   *Generation*: turn the act into a sentence, then speech (ch. 10).
:::

::: ex
[Code 11.2 — A retrieval-based chatbot]{.tag}

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

faq = {"How do I reset my password?": "Use the 'forgot password' link on the login page.",
       "When is the library open?": "From 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday.",
       "How can I book a meeting room?": "Rooms are booked on the intranet, up to two weeks ahead.",
       "Where do I submit the project report?": "Upload the PDF on the course page before the deadline."}
questions = list(faq)
vec = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english").fit(questions)

def respond(user_turn, threshold=0.2):
    """Retrieval-based chatbot: answer of the most similar stored question, or a fallback."""
    sims = cosine_similarity(vec.transform([user_turn]), vec.transform(questions))[0]
    best = sims.argmax()
    score = round(float(sims[best]), 2)
    return (faq[questions[best]] if score >= threshold else "Sorry, could you rephrase?"), score

for turn in ["I forgot my password", "is the library open on sunday", "what is the meaning of life"]:
    print(turn, "->", respond(turn))
```

The password question is matched (similarity 0.71) and the off-topic one falls back. The library question matches with similarity 1.0, yet the answer does not say whether it opens on Sunday: retrieval returns canned text and cannot reason.
:::

### 11.2 LLM-based chatbots and retrieval

An LLM assistant (ch. 7) conditions on the whole conversation, marked with roles (system, user, assistant). It answers any request fluently, but can state false facts with confidence: *hallucination*.

::: def
[Definition 11.3 — Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)]{.tag} A retriever scores documents $z$ of a collection against the query $x$ and keeps the top $K$; the generator conditions on them:
$$
P(y \mid x) \approx \sum_{z \in \mathrm{top}\text{-}K(x)} P(z \mid x)\, P(y \mid x, z) .
$$

Lewis and coauthors (2020) trained both jointly; often the passages are simply pasted into the prompt.
:::

### 11.3 Code generation

Code can be executed, so it is judged by passing unit tests. HumanEval (Chen and coauthors, 2021) has 164 hand-written Python problems with tests.

::: def
[Definition 11.4 — pass@k]{.tag} For a problem, pass@k is the probability that at least one of $k$ independent samples from the model passes all the tests. If one sample passes with probability $p$, then $\text{pass@}k = 1 - (1 - p)^k$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 11.5 — An unbiased estimator of pass@k]{.tag} Draw $n \geq k$ samples, of which $c$ pass. Then
$$
\widehat{\text{pass@}k} = 1 - \binom{n - c}{k} \Big/ \binom{n}{k}
$$
is an unbiased estimator of pass@k (Chen and coauthors, 2021).

::: proof
Given the $n$ samples, the ratio of binomials is the probability that a uniformly random $k$-subset of them has no passing sample; the estimator is the probability that it has one.

A uniformly random $k$-subset of $n$ i.i.d. samples is itself $k$ i.i.d. samples, so the average over the samples is exactly $1 - (1 - p)^k$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Code 11.6 — Unbiased versus plug-in estimates]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from math import comb
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def pass_at_k(n, c, k):
    """Unbiased estimator of pass@k from n samples with c correct (Chen et al., 2021)."""
    return 1.0 if n - c < k else 1.0 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k)

p_true, n, k = 0.1, 20, 5                                # each sample passes the tests w.p. 0.1
target = 1 - (1 - p_true) ** k                           # true pass@5
c = rng.binomial(n, p_true, size=20000)                  # 20,000 problems, n samples each
unbiased = np.mean([pass_at_k(n, ci, k) for ci in c])
plug_in = np.mean(1 - (1 - c / n) ** k)                  # naive plug-in estimator
print(f"true pass@5 {target:.4f}   unbiased {unbiased:.4f}   plug-in {plug_in:.4f}")
```

The true pass@5 is 0.4095; the unbiased estimator averages 0.4113, the plug-in 0.3796, biased downwards because $p \mapsto 1 - (1-p)^k$ is concave.
:::

### 11.4 Agents

::: def
[Definition 11.7 — Agent loop]{.tag} An LLM agent repeats: read the context (task, history, last observation); generate a reasoning step and an action, a tool call (search, code execution, file edit); append the tool's output. It stops with a final answer. ReAct (Yao and coauthors, 2023) interleaves reasoning and actions this way.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 11.8 — Errors compound]{.tag} If each of $n$ steps succeeds independently with probability $q$ and the task needs all of them, the task succeeds with probability $q^n$. With $q = 0.95$ and $n = 20$ steps,
$$
q^n = 0.95^{20} \approx 0.36 .
$$
::::

Hence agents check their work (run tests, read errors, retry), and benchmarks such as SWE-bench (Jimenez and coauthors, 2024), built from real GitHub issues, score whole tasks. [Large Language Models for Code and Proof](../s2-llm-code-proof/index.html) goes further.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 11

-   Task-oriented dialogue chains understanding (slot filling), state tracking, a policy and generation.
-   Retrieval bots are rigid, LLM chatbots hallucinate, RAG grounds them in documents.
-   Code is judged by tests; pass@k has an unbiased estimator (Proposition 11.5).
-   Agents loop between reasoning, tool calls and observations; per-step errors compound geometrically.
:::

## 12. Evaluation: comparing human and machine performance {#ch12}

Every chapter ended with a metric. This one asks when a difference between two systems, or between a system and humans, is real: it measures human agreement, tests significance, and lists how scores mislead.

### 12.1 Human agreement as a reference

::: def
[Definition 12.1 — Cohen's kappa]{.tag} Two annotators label the same $n$ items. Let $p_o$ be their observed agreement and $p_e = \sum_k p_k^{(1)} p_k^{(2)}$ the agreement expected by chance from their label frequencies. Then
$$
\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e} .
$$

$\kappa = 1$ for perfect agreement and $\kappa = 0$ for chance-level agreement (Cohen, 1960).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 12.2 — Scoring against a noisy reference]{.tag} Let the reference label be wrong with probability $\varepsilon$, and the system be right with probability $a$, independently, among $K$ classes. Suppose both pick a wrong label uniformly among the $K - 1$ wrong ones. Then the measured accuracy is
$$
\tilde a = a (1 - \varepsilon) + (1 - a)\, \frac{\varepsilon}{K - 1} .
$$

::: proof
The system agrees with the reference when both are right, with probability $a(1 - \varepsilon)$, or when both are wrong with the same label: probability $(1 - a)\,\varepsilon$ times $1 / (K - 1)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A perfect system scores only $1 - \varepsilon$. Matching the agreement between two humans is the natural definition of “human parity”, but it hides which errors each makes.

::: ex
[Example 12.3 — Two claims of human parity]{.tag} Xiong and coauthors (2016) reported a WER of 5.9 % on Switchboard conversational speech, equal to that of professional transcribers; Saon and coauthors (2017) then measured careful human transcription at 5.1 %. Hassan and coauthors (2018) claimed parity for Chinese–English news translation; Läubli, Sennrich and Volk (2018) found that translators reading whole documents still preferred human output. The verdict depends on the humans and the protocol.
:::

### 12.2 Is the difference significant?

::: def
[Definition 12.4 — Paired bootstrap (Koehn, 2004)]{.tag} Score systems A and B on the same $n$ items. Resample $n$ items with replacement many times and recompute the difference each time. The 2.5 % and 97.5 % quantiles give a 95 % interval; the share of resamples where B is not worse says how often A's advantage vanishes.
:::

::: ex
[Code 12.5 — Agreement, human baseline and bootstrap]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

n = 500                                                  # 500 items, 3 sentiment classes
gold = rng.choice(3, size=n, p=[0.5, 0.3, 0.2])
def annotate(acc):                                       # keep the label w.p. acc, else random
    return np.where(rng.random(n) < acc, gold, rng.choice(3, size=n))
ann1, ann2, sys_a, sys_b = annotate(0.85), annotate(0.85), annotate(0.80), annotate(0.76)

p_o = np.mean(ann1 == ann2)                              # observed agreement
p_e = sum(np.mean(ann1 == k) * np.mean(ann2 == k) for k in range(3))   # chance agreement
print(f"annotators: agreement {p_o:.3f}, kappa {(p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e):.3f} "
      f"(sklearn {cohen_kappa_score(ann1, ann2):.3f})")

ref = ann1                                               # evaluate systems against one annotator
acc_a, acc_b = np.mean(sys_a == ref), np.mean(sys_b == ref)
delta = acc_a - acc_b
idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(10000, n))                # paired bootstrap (Koehn, 2004)
deltas = (sys_a[idx] == ref[idx]).mean(1) - (sys_b[idx] == ref[idx]).mean(1)
print(f"accuracy vs annotator 1: A {acc_a:.3f}, B {acc_b:.3f}, annotator 2 {np.mean(ann2 == ref):.3f}")
print(f"delta {delta:.3f}, 95% bootstrap interval [{np.quantile(deltas, 0.025):.3f}, {np.quantile(deltas, 0.975):.3f}], "
      f"share of resamples with delta <= 0: {np.mean(deltas <= 0):.3f}")
```

The annotators agree on 82.0 % of items, $\kappa = 0.724$. Against annotator 1, system A scores 80.2 %, near annotator 2's 82.0 %, and B 77.0 %. A's advantage of 3.2 points has the 95 % interval $[-1.2, 7.6]$: on 500 items it is not established.
:::

### 12.3 How benchmark scores mislead

-   **Artefacts.** A classifier that reads only the hypothesis of SNLI pairs, never the premise, predicts the label for about 67 % of them (Gururangan and coauthors, 2018).
-   **Saturation and contamination.** Benchmarks are solved within years, and public test sets leak into pretraining data; dynamic benchmarks collected with models in the loop respond (Kiela and coauthors, 2021).
-   **Automatic judges.** An LLM grader agrees well with human preferences but favours the first position, longer answers and its own outputs (Zheng and coauthors, 2023).
-   **Human evaluation.** MOS (ch. 10) and translation assessments need trained raters, randomised order and enough items for confidence intervals.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 12

-   Kappa measures human agreement; reference noise caps the measurable accuracy at $1 - \varepsilon$ (Proposition 12.2).
-   “Human parity” claims depend on which humans, which data and which protocol.
-   Report confidence intervals: a paired bootstrap on the same items is simple and standard.
-   Scores can reflect artefacts, contamination or judge biases rather than ability.
:::

## 13. Complements for self-study {#ch13}

This chapter completes four topics of the course with material that does not fit the 21 hours: a better smoothing method, the derivation of Baum–Welch, the RNN transducer, and the closed form behind DPO. Each section can be read after the chapter it extends.

### 13.1 Kneser–Ney smoothing (extends ch. 1)

Add-k smoothing gives the same share to every unseen word. Kneser and Ney (1995) observed that the backup distribution should favour words that appear after *many different* contexts: “Francisco” is frequent, but almost always after “San”, so it is a poor guess after a new context.

::: def
[Definition 13.1 — Interpolated Kneser–Ney for bigrams]{.tag} With a discount $0 < d < 1$, let $N_{1+}(u\,\bullet)$ be the number of distinct words seen after $u$, $N_{1+}(\bullet\,w)$ the number of distinct words seen before $w$, and $N_{1+}(\bullet\,\bullet)$ the number of distinct bigrams. Then
$$
P_{\mathrm{KN}}(w \mid u) = \frac{\max(c(u, w) - d,\ 0)}{c(u)} + \lambda(u)\, P_{\mathrm{cont}}(w),
$$
$$
\lambda(u) = \frac{d\, N_{1+}(u\,\bullet)}{c(u)}, \qquad P_{\mathrm{cont}}(w) = \frac{N_{1+}(\bullet\,w)}{N_{1+}(\bullet\,\bullet)} .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 13.2 — Kneser–Ney is normalised]{.tag} For every context $u$ with $c(u) > 0$,
$$
\sum_{w} P_{\mathrm{KN}}(w \mid u) = 1 .
$$

::: proof
Each of the $N_{1+}(u\,\bullet)$ seen bigrams loses exactly $d$, because counts are integers and $d < 1$. The first terms therefore sum to
$$
\frac{c(u) - d\, N_{1+}(u\,\bullet)}{c(u)} = 1 - \lambda(u) .
$$

The continuation probabilities sum to one, since every bigram type has exactly one second word. Adding $\lambda(u)$ times 1 gives 1. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Code 13.3 — Kneser–Ney on the corpus of Code 1.8]{.tag}

```python
import math
from collections import Counter

train = ["<s> the cat sat on the mat </s>", "<s> the dog sat on the log </s>",
         "<s> the cat saw the dog </s>"]
test = ["<s> the dog sat on the mat </s>", "<s> the dog saw the cat </s>"]
tok = [s.split() for s in train]
big = Counter((u, w) for s in tok for u, w in zip(s, s[1:]))
ctx = Counter(u for s in tok for u in s[:-1])
followers = Counter(u for (u, w) in big)                 # N1+(u .): distinct words after u
preceders = Counter(w for (u, w) in big)                 # N1+(. w): distinct words before w
n_types = len(big)                                       # N1+(. .): distinct bigram types

def p_kn(w, u, d=0.75):
    """Interpolated Kneser-Ney bigram probability."""
    p_cont = preceders[w] / n_types                      # continuation probability
    lam = d * followers[u] / ctx[u]                      # mass freed by discounting
    return max(big[u, w] - d, 0) / ctx[u] + lam * p_cont

V = sorted({w for s in tok for w in s} - {"<s>"})
print("sums to one:", all(abs(sum(p_kn(w, u) for w in V) - 1) < 1e-12 for u in ctx))
for d in [0.5, 0.75, 0.9]:
    lp = [math.log(p_kn(v, u, d)) for s in test for u, v in zip(s.split(), s.split()[1:])]
    print(f"Kneser-Ney d = {d}: perplexity {math.exp(-sum(lp) / len(lp)):.2f}")
```

The distributions sum to one, and the perplexity is 3.07 for $d = 0.5$, below the best add-k value of Code 1.8 (3.25). Chen and Goodman (1999) found modified Kneser–Ney, with three discounts, the best n-gram smoothing on large corpora.
:::

### 13.2 Baum–Welch as expectation–maximisation (extends ch. 3)

Write $\theta = (\pi, A, B)$ for the parameters and $q$ for the hidden path. EM maximises at each step the expected complete log-likelihood
$$
Q(\theta', \theta) = \sum_{q} P(q \mid O; \theta) \log P(q, O; \theta') .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 13.4 — EM never decreases the likelihood]{.tag} For all parameters $\theta, \theta'$,
$$
\log P(O; \theta') - \log P(O; \theta) \geq Q(\theta', \theta) - Q(\theta, \theta) .
$$

So choosing $\theta'$ that maximises $Q(\cdot, \theta)$ gives $P(O; \theta') \geq P(O; \theta)$.

::: proof
Write $w_q = P(q \mid O; \theta)$, a law on paths. By Jensen's inequality for the concave logarithm,
$$
\log \frac{P(O; \theta')}{P(O; \theta)} = \log \sum_q w_q \frac{P(q, O; \theta')}{P(q, O; \theta)} \geq \sum_q w_q \log \frac{P(q, O; \theta')}{P(q, O; \theta)} .
$$

The right-hand side is $Q(\theta', \theta) - Q(\theta, \theta)$. Since $\theta' = \theta$ is a candidate, the maximiser makes it non-negative. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 13.5 — The M-step of Baum–Welch]{.tag} The maximiser of $Q(\cdot, \theta)$ is given by the updates of Theorem 3.8.

::: proof
The logarithm of the joint law of Definition 3.3 is a sum of terms $\log \pi_{q_1}$, $\log A_{q_{t-1} q_t}$ and $\log b_{q_t}(o_t)$. Its expectation under the posterior is
$$
Q = \sum_i \gamma_1(i) \log \pi'_i + \sum_{t < T} \sum_{i, j} \xi_t(i, j) \log A'_{ij} + \sum_t \sum_i \gamma_t(i) \log b'_i(o_t) .
$$

The three groups of parameters separate, and each row of the transition and emission matrices is a separate law. For a law $p$ and non-negative weights $n_k$, Gibbs' inequality (or a Lagrange multiplier) gives the maximiser of a weighted log-likelihood:
$$
\arg\max_p \sum_k n_k \log p_k = \Big( \frac{n_k}{\sum_j n_j} \Big)_k .
$$

Apply it three times:

-   to the initial law, with the weights $\gamma_1(i)$;
-   to row $i$ of the transition matrix, with the weights $\xi_t(i, j)$ summed over $t$;
-   to row $i$ of the emission matrix, with the weights $\gamma_t(i)$ summed over the times where $o_t = v$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Code 13.6 — Baum–Welch on 500 sampled observations]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pi = np.array([0.8, 0.2]); A = np.array([[0.6, 0.4], [0.5, 0.5]])
B = np.array([[0.2, 0.4, 0.4], [0.5, 0.4, 0.1]])
q, obs = rng.choice(2, p=pi), []
for t in range(500):                                   # sample 500 observations
    obs.append(rng.choice(3, p=B[q])); q = rng.choice(2, p=A[q])
obs = np.array(obs)

def forward_backward(pi, A, B, obs):
    T, K = len(obs), len(pi)
    alpha, beta, c = np.zeros((T, K)), np.ones((T, K)), np.zeros(T)
    alpha[0] = pi * B[:, obs[0]]; c[0] = alpha[0].sum(); alpha[0] /= c[0]
    for t in range(1, T):                              # scaled forward pass
        alpha[t] = (alpha[t - 1] @ A) * B[:, obs[t]]; c[t] = alpha[t].sum(); alpha[t] /= c[t]
    for t in range(T - 2, -1, -1):                     # scaled backward pass
        beta[t] = A @ (B[:, obs[t + 1]] * beta[t + 1]) / c[t + 1]
    gamma = alpha * beta                               # P(q_t = i | O)
    xi = alpha[:-1, :, None] * A[None] * (B[:, obs[1:]].T * beta[1:])[:, None, :] / c[1:, None, None]
    return gamma, xi, np.log(c).sum()                  # log P(O) = sum_t log c_t

pi_h, A_h = np.array([0.5, 0.5]), np.array([[0.7, 0.3], [0.3, 0.7]])
B_h = np.array([[0.3, 0.3, 0.4], [0.4, 0.3, 0.3]])
for it in range(30):                                   # Baum-Welch = EM
    gamma, xi, ll = forward_backward(pi_h, A_h, B_h, obs)
    if it % 5 == 0:
        print(f"iteration {it:2d}  log P(O) = {ll:.3f}")
    pi_h = gamma[0]
    A_h = xi.sum(0) / xi.sum((0, 2))[:, None]
    B_h = np.stack([gamma[obs == o].sum(0) for o in range(3)], 1) / gamma.sum(0)[:, None]
print("true model: log P(O) =", round(forward_backward(pi, A, B, obs)[2], 3))
print("estimated B:\n", B_h.round(2))
```

The log-likelihood rises from −553.8 to −541.1 in 25 iterations, above the −542.9 of the true model: maximum likelihood fits the sample. The estimated emission rows, (0.26, 0.36, 0.38) and (0.47, 0.39, 0.14), are close to the true ones. Scaling each $\alpha_t$ by its sum $c_t$ avoids underflow on long sequences.
:::


### 13.3 The RNN transducer (extends ch. 10)

CTC predicts each frame independently of the labels already emitted. The RNN transducer (Graves, 2012) adds a prediction network over the previous labels, which acts as an internal language model.

::: def
[Definition 13.7 — RNN transducer]{.tag} An encoder gives frame vectors $f_t$, and a prediction network gives a vector $g_u$ for each prefix of $u$ labels. A joint network outputs, at each lattice node $(t, u)$, a law $P(k \mid t, u)$ over the labels plus the blank.

From node $(t, u)$, a blank moves to the next frame and the label $y_{u+1}$ moves to the next output:
$$
(t, u) \xrightarrow{\ \varnothing\ } (t + 1, u), \qquad (t, u) \xrightarrow{\ y_{u+1}\ } (t, u + 1) .
$$

The probability of $y$ sums over all such paths from $(1, 0)$ that end with a blank at $(T, U)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 13.8 — Transducer forward recursion]{.tag} With $\alpha(1, 0) = 1$,
$$
\alpha(t, u) = \alpha(t - 1, u)\, P(\varnothing \mid t - 1, u) + \alpha(t, u - 1)\, P(y_u \mid t, u - 1),
$$
and $P(y \mid x) = \alpha(T, U)\, P(\varnothing \mid T, U)$, in $O(TU)$ operations.

::: proof
Every path reaching $(t, u)$ arrives either by a blank from $(t - 1, u)$ or by the label $y_u$ from $(t, u - 1)$; the two sets are disjoint. Proposition 0.6 on the lattice graph gives the recursion, and the final blank closes the path. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Code 13.9 — The transducer recursion against enumeration]{.tag}

```python
import itertools
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T, y, K = 4, [1, 2], 3                                   # 4 frames, target "a b", symbols: blank=0, a=1, b=2
U = len(y)
logits = rng.normal(size=(T, U + 1, K))                  # joint network output at lattice node (t, u)
logp = logits - np.log(np.exp(logits).sum(-1, keepdims=True))

alpha = np.full((T, U + 1), -np.inf); alpha[0, 0] = 0.0
for t in range(T):
    for u in range(U + 1):
        terms = []
        if t > 0: terms.append(alpha[t - 1, u] + logp[t - 1, u, 0])          # blank: next frame
        if u > 0: terms.append(alpha[t, u - 1] + logp[t, u - 1, y[u - 1]])   # label: next output
        if terms: alpha[t, u] = np.logaddexp.reduce(terms)
forward = alpha[T - 1, U] + logp[T - 1, U, 0]            # final blank

paths = []                                               # brute force: place U labels among T-1+U steps
for pos in itertools.combinations(range(T - 1 + U), U):
    t, u, lp = 0, 0, 0.0
    for step in range(T - 1 + U):
        if step in pos: lp += logp[t, u, y[u]]; u += 1
        else: lp += logp[t, u, 0]; t += 1
    paths.append(lp + logp[t, u, 0])
print(f"{len(paths)} paths; log P(y|x): forward {forward:.4f}, brute force {np.logaddexp.reduce(paths):.4f}")
```

There are $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ paths, and both computations give $\log P(y \mid x) = -4.3427$.
:::

### 13.4 The KL-regularised optimum and DPO (extends ch. 7)

RLHF trains a reward model $r$ on human comparisons with the Bradley–Terry likelihood
$$
P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma\big(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)\big),
$$
then optimises the policy against it.

::: def
[Definition 13.10 — KL-regularised preference optimisation]{.tag} For each prompt $x$, the policy $\pi$ maximises
$$
J(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)} \big[ r(x, y) \big] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\big),
$$
where $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the instruction-tuned model and $\beta > 0$ sets how far the policy may move (Ouyang and coauthors, 2022).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 13.11 — Closed-form optimum]{.tag} The maximiser of $J$ is
$$
\pi^*(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\, e^{r(x, y) / \beta}, \qquad Z(x) = \sum_y \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\, e^{r(x, y) / \beta} .
$$

::: proof
Expand the KL divergence and group the terms:
$$
J(\pi) = -\beta \sum_y \pi(y \mid x) \log \frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\, e^{r(x, y)/\beta}} = -\beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi^*) + \beta \log Z(x) .
$$

The last term does not depend on $\pi$, and the KL divergence is minimal, equal to zero, at $\pi = \pi^*$ (Proposition 0.2). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Inverting the optimum gives the reward as a function of the policy:
$$
r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x) .
$$

In the Bradley–Terry likelihood only the difference of two rewards for the same prompt appears, so $Z(x)$ cancels. Fitting the policy directly to the preference pairs gives the DPO loss (Rafailov and coauthors, 2023):

::: key
[Key result — the DPO loss]{.tag}
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\Big( \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)} \Big)
$$
:::

No reward model and no sampling are needed: DPO is a logistic regression on pairs, whose “features” are log-probability ratios.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 13

-   Kneser–Ney backs off to a continuation probability: how many contexts a word completes, not how frequent it is.
-   EM ascends a lower bound that touches the likelihood; for HMMs the M-step is fractional-count estimation.
-   The RNN transducer replaces the CTC independence assumption by a lattice over frames and emitted labels.
-   The KL-regularised optimum is a reweighted reference policy; inverting it turns preference learning into the DPO logistic loss.
:::

## 14. Research directions and open problems {#ch14}

This chapter is for self-study. It points to active lines of research that extend the course, each with a few papers to start from and the questions that remain open.

### 14.1 Spoken language models without text

Generative spoken language modelling (Lakhotia and coauthors, 2021) chains the pieces of ch. 10 without any text: self-supervised speech features (HuBERT or wav2vec 2.0), k-means discrete units, a transformer language model over the units (ch. 7), and a unit-to-speech synthesiser. The model continues a spoken prompt in speech.

-   Work by Nguyen and coauthors (2023) extends the idea to two-channel conversations, where the model generates turn-taking, overlaps and laughter that a transcript would lose.
-   Spirit LM (Nguyen and coauthors, 2024) interleaves speech units and text tokens in one model, to transfer knowledge from text to speech.
-   Dupoux (2018) argues for reverse-engineering the infant language learner: children learn to speak from raw audio and interaction, with far less data than a text model, and the gap is a measurable scientific question.

Open problems: discrete units capture phonetic content well but prosody and meaning poorly; spoken models still lag far behind text models of the same size in coherence; and data efficiency is nowhere near that of children.

### 14.2 Long contexts and sub-quadratic architectures

Attention costs $O(T^2)$ in the sequence length (ch. 6). Structured state-space models (Gu, Goel and Ré, 2022) and their selective variant Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) process sequences in linear time with a recurrent state. Hyena (Poli and coauthors, 2023) replaces attention by long implicit convolutions interleaved with gating.

Open problems: Jelassi and coauthors (2024) prove and observe that fixed-size recurrent states are worse than attention at copying long inputs, and hybrid models that mix attention and recurrent layers are an active compromise. Which tasks need full attention, and how much, is not settled.

### 14.3 Multilingual and document-level translation

Most of the world's languages have little parallel text. Massively multilingual models such as NLLB (NLLB Team, 2022), covering 200 languages, and open multilingual LLMs such as BLOOM (BigScience Workshop, 2022) share parameters across languages so that low-resource ones benefit from high-resource ones.

Sentence-level systems ignore context. Bawden and coauthors (2018) built contrastive test sets for coreference and lexical cohesion across sentences: a model that sees only the current sentence scores at chance on them, and only some ways of feeding it the previous sentence help. Freitag and coauthors (2021) showed with expert MQM annotations that crowd ratings and BLEU can rank systems differently from professional translators.

Open problems: reliable evaluation for languages without references or expert raters; translation of whole documents with consistent terminology; measuring and reducing gender and cultural bias in outputs.

### 14.4 Affect and interaction

In conversation, opinions are spread over turns, carried by prosody as much as by words, and addressed to a partner. Clavel and Callejas (2016) review how sentiment analysis moved from opinion mining in product reviews to human–agent interaction, where a virtual agent must detect the user's attitude in real time and respond to it.

Open problems: labels of social and emotional phenomena have low inter-annotator agreement (ch. 12), so the ceiling of supervised learning is low; multimodal models must align words, prosody and gestures in time; and an agent's reaction changes the user's next turn, which static datasets cannot capture.

### 14.5 Evaluation that keeps pace

As benchmarks saturate and leak into pretraining data, the field is moving to dynamic benchmarks (Kiela and coauthors, 2021), human preference arenas and LLM judges (Zheng and coauthors, 2023), and task-level evaluations of agents such as SWE-bench (Jimenez and coauthors, 2024).

Open problems: detecting contamination without access to the training data; calibrated LLM judges whose biases are measured and corrected; and comparisons with humans that specify which humans, with what training and time, as ch. 12 requires.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 14

-   Spoken language models learn from audio alone; their gap with text models and with infants is open.
-   Sub-quadratic architectures trade attention's exact recall for linear cost; hybrids are an active compromise.
-   Translation research targets low-resource languages, document context and expert evaluation.
-   Sentiment in interaction, contamination-free evaluation and agent reliability remain open measurement problems.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

The exercises are sorted by level: ★ applies the course, ★★ combines results or proves a short statement, ★★★ is open-ended or research-flavoured. Exercises 13, 18 and 19 are computational.

1.  **★ Perplexity by hand.** With the training corpus of Code 1.8 and add-one smoothing ($|V| = 9$), compute the six bigram probabilities of “`<s>` the dog saw the cat `</s>`” and the perplexity of the sentence.

    *Solution*: each probability is $(c(u, w) + 1)/(c(u) + 9)$. In order, the six bigrams have probabilities
    $$
    \frac{4}{12}, \quad \frac{3}{15}, \quad \frac{1}{11}, \quad \frac{2}{10}, \quad \frac{3}{15}, \quad \frac{1}{11},
    $$
    where “dog saw” and “cat `</s>`” are unseen.

    The log-probability is $-10.72$ over 6 predictions, so
    $$
    \mathrm{PP} = e^{10.72 / 6} \approx 5.97 .
    $$

2.  **★ Frames, bins and mels.** Telephone speech is sampled at 8 kHz. With 25 ms windows, a 10 ms hop and a DFT of size 256: how many samples per window, how many frames in 2 s, what is the bin spacing, and what is the mel value of the Nyquist frequency?

    *Solution*: 200 samples per window and 80 per hop; $1 + \lfloor (16000 - 200)/80 \rfloor = 198$ frames; bins every $8000/256 = 31.25$ Hz; the Nyquist frequency is 4000 Hz and
    $$
    \mathrm{mel}(4000) = 2595 \log_{10}(1 + 4000/700) \approx 2146 .
    $$

3.  **★ Viterbi by hand.** With the HMM of Code 3.6, observe 1, 3, 1 ice creams. Run the forward and Viterbi recursions and give $P(O)$ and the best path.

    *Solution*: $\alpha_1 = \delta_1 = (0.16, 0.10)$; $\alpha_2 = (0.0584, 0.0114)$, $\alpha_3 = (0.008148, 0.01453)$, so $P(O) = 0.022678$.

    For Viterbi, $\delta_2 = (0.0384, 0.0064)$ and $\delta_3 = (0.004608, 0.00768)$. The best path is hot, hot, cold, with probability $0.00768$, confirmed by enumerating the 8 paths.

4.  **★ BIO tags and span F1.** In “The University of Paris-Saclay hired Ada Lovelace in Orsay .” the gold entities are an organisation (“University of Paris-Saclay”), a person and a location. A tagger outputs `O B-ORG I-ORG O O B-PER I-PER O B-LOC O`. Write the gold tags, and compute token accuracy and span F1.

    *Solution*: gold `O B-ORG I-ORG I-ORG O B-PER I-PER O B-LOC O`. One token differs, so the accuracy is 90 %. The predicted organisation “University of” has the wrong boundary: 2 correct spans out of 3 predicted and 3 gold, so $P = R = F_1 = 2/3$.

5.  **★ BLEU by hand.** Compute BLEU with $N = 2$ for the hypothesis “the cat the cat on the mat” against the reference “the cat is on the mat”.

    *Solution*: clipped unigram matches: “the” 2 (not 3), “cat” 1 (not 2), “on” 1, “mat” 1, so $p_1 = 5/7$. Bigram matches: “the cat” once, “on the”, “the mat”, so $p_2 = 3/6$. The hypothesis is longer than the reference, so BP = 1 and
    $$
    \mathrm{BLEU}_2 = \sqrt{5/7 \cdot 1/2} \approx 0.598 .
    $$

6.  **★ CTC paths and WER.** (a) With the blank written “-”, list the paths of length 3 that CTC collapses to “ab”, then those that collapse to “aa”. (b) Compute the WER of “a meeting starts noon today” against “the meeting starts at noon”.

    *Solution*: (a) `-ab`, `a-b`, `ab-`, `aab`, `abb`: five paths. For “aa” only `a-a` works, since the repeated label needs a blank.

    (b) An optimal alignment has one substitution (the → a), one deletion (at) and one insertion (today), on 5 reference words: WER = 3/5 = 60 %.

7.  **★ Cohen's kappa.** Two annotators label 100 reviews. Both say positive 40 times, both negative 30 times; A says positive and B negative 20 times, the reverse 10 times. Compute $p_o$, $p_e$ and $\kappa$.

    *Solution*: $p_o = 0.70$. A says positive 60 % of the time and B 50 %, so $p_e = 0.6 \cdot 0.5 + 0.4 \cdot 0.5 = 0.50$, and
    $$
    \kappa = \frac{0.70 - 0.50}{1 - 0.50} = 0.40 .
    $$

8.  **★★ Forward–backward identities.** For an HMM, prove that $\sum_i \alpha_t(i)\, \beta_t(i) = P(O)$ for every $t$, and deduce the formula of $\gamma_t(i)$ in ch. 3. Then show that the Viterbi recursion is the forward recursion in the max-product semiring.

    *Solution*: by the Markov property, given $q_t = i$ the future observations are independent of the past ones and of $o_t$. Hence
    $$
    \alpha_t(i)\, \beta_t(i) = P(o_{1:t}, q_t = i)\, P(o_{t+1:T} \mid q_t = i) = P(O, q_t = i) .
    $$

    Summing over $i$ gives $P(O)$, and dividing by $P(O)$ gives $\gamma_t(i) = P(q_t = i \mid O)$. Replacing sums by maxima in the proof of Theorem 3.4 is legitimate because $\max$ distributes over products of non-negative numbers (Definition 0.5).

9.  **★★ A CRF without transitions.** Show that a linear-chain CRF whose features depend only on $(y_t, x, t)$, not on $y_{t-1}$, factorises into independent softmax classifiers, one per token. What does Theorem 4.4 become?

    *Solution*: the exponent is a sum of terms $\theta^\top f(y_t, x, t)$, so the numerator is a product over $t$ and $Z(x)$, a sum over all sequences, is the product of the per-token normalisers (distributivity). Hence $p(y \mid x) = \prod_t \mathrm{softmax}_{y_t}$. The gradient becomes, token by token, observed minus expected features: the gradient of multinomial logistic regression (Proposition 0.4). Transitions are what make the CRF more than a per-token classifier.

10. **★★ SGNS at the optimum.** A pair is seen $c(w, u) = 30$ times, with $c(w) = 300$, $c(u) = 1000$, $D = 10^6$ and $k = 5$ negatives. (a) What inner product does Theorem 5.5 predict? (b) What happens to pairs never seen together, and how does PPMI handle the same issue?

    *Solution*: (a) The PMI is
    $$
    \log \frac{30 \cdot 10^6}{300 \cdot 1000} = \log 100 \approx 4.61,
    $$
    so the optimal inner product is $4.61 - \log 5 \approx 3.00$.

    (b) With $c(w, u) = 0$ the objective $k\, c(w) c(u) D^{-1} \log \sigma(-s)$ increases as $s \to -\infty$: the unconstrained optimum is $-\infty$, like $\mathrm{PMI} = \log 0$. Low dimension keeps it finite in SGNS; PPMI truncates negative values at 0.

11. **★★ Gradients through time.** (a) For the scalar RNN $h_t = \tanh(w h_{t-1} + x_t)$ with $w = 0.9$, bound $|\partial h_{50} / \partial h_0|$. (b) Compare with an LSTM whose forget gate stays at $f_t = 0.99$, along the cell path. (c) Why does the transformer not have this problem across positions?

    *Solution*: (a) Proposition 6.2 gives at most $0.9^{50} \approx 0.005$. (b) Along the cell, the factor is $0.99^{50} \approx 0.61$: the signal survives. (c) Any two positions are connected by one attention step, so the path length between them is 1, not their distance; the price is the $O(T^2)$ cost.

12. **★★ pass@k.** (a) With $n = 10$ samples of which $c = 2$ pass, compute the estimate of pass@5. (b) Show that for $k = 1$ the estimator is $c / n$. (c) Prove that the plug-in estimator $1 - (1 - c/n)^k$ is biased downwards.

    *Solution*: (a) $1 - \binom{8}{5} / \binom{10}{5} = 1 - 56/252 \approx 0.778$. (b) $\binom{n-c}{1} / \binom{n}{1} = (n - c)/n$. (c) $g(p) = 1 - (1 - p)^k$ is concave, and $c/n$ is unbiased for $p$, so by Jensen
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\big[g(c/n)\big] \leq g\big(\mathbb{E}[c/n]\big) = g(p) .
    $$

13. **★★ CTC in log space, vectorised (Python).** Rewrite the CTC recursion of Code 10.5 without the inner loop over $s$, check it against `torch.nn.functional.ctc_loss` on 50 frames and a label of length 8, then decode greedily.

    *Solution*: shift the vector $\alpha$ by one and by two positions, mask the forbidden skips once, and combine the three with a log-sum-exp.

    ```python
    import torch
    torch.set_num_threads(1); torch.manual_seed(0)

    def ctc_nll(logp, y, blank=0):
        """CTC negative log-likelihood, vectorised over the extended label sequence."""
        z = torch.full((2 * len(y) + 1,), blank, dtype=torch.long)
        z[1::2] = torch.tensor(y)
        S = len(z)
        skip = torch.zeros(S, dtype=torch.bool)
        skip[2:] = (z[2:] != blank) & (z[2:] != z[:-2])        # allowed jumps s-2 -> s
        alpha = torch.full((S,), float("-inf"))
        alpha[:2] = logp[0, z[:2]]
        for t in range(1, logp.shape[0]):
            a1 = torch.cat([torch.tensor([float("-inf")]), alpha[:-1]])
            a2 = torch.cat([torch.tensor([float("-inf")] * 2), alpha[:-2]])
            a2 = torch.where(skip, a2, torch.tensor(float("-inf")))
            alpha = torch.logsumexp(torch.stack([alpha, a1, a2]), 0) + logp[t, z]
        return -torch.logsumexp(alpha[-2:], 0)

    T, C = 50, 6
    logp = torch.randn(T, C).log_softmax(-1)
    y = [1, 3, 3, 2, 5, 1, 1, 4]
    ref = torch.nn.functional.ctc_loss(logp[:, None], torch.tensor([y]), [T], [len(y)], reduction="sum")
    print(f"ours {ctc_nll(logp, y):.4f}   torch {ref:.4f}")
    best = logp.argmax(-1).tolist()                           # greedy decoding: best symbol per frame
    decoded = [k for i, k in enumerate(best) if (i == 0 or k != best[i - 1]) and k != 0]
    print("greedy output length", len(decoded))
    ```

    Both give 63.8471. On random scores, greedy decoding outputs 38 symbols instead of 8: an untrained network has no reason to emit blanks.

14. **★★ Naive Bayes and negation by hand.** Train multinomial naive Bayes with add-one smoothing on four documents: (+) “good movie”, (+) “great plot”, (−) “not good”, (−) “boring plot”. Compute the log-odds of “not good” and of “not great”, and explain the second result.

    *Solution*: each class has 4 tokens and the vocabulary 6 words, so each estimate is $(c + 1)/10$. For “not good”, the log-odds are $\log(0.1/0.2) + \log(0.2/0.2) = -0.69$: negative, correct.

    For “not great”, they are $\log(0.1/0.2) + \log(0.2/0.1) = 0$: a tie. The model adds a fixed weight per word and cannot learn that “not” flips “great”; a bigram feature “not great”, or the NOT_ marking of Code 9.4, would.

15. **★★ Temperature.** Let $p_T = \mathrm{softmax}(z / T)$ with distinct logits. Prove that $p_T$ tends to the one-hot vector of $\arg\max_k z_k$ as $T \to 0$, to the uniform law as $T \to \infty$, and that its entropy increases with $T$.

    *Solution*: divide numerator and denominator by $e^{z_{\max}/T}$; every other term is $e^{-(z_{\max} - z_k)/T} \to 0$. As $T \to \infty$, every $e^{z_k/T} \to 1$. With $b = 1/T$, $H = \log Z(b) - b\, \mathbb{E}_p[z]$, and differentiating,
    $$
    \frac{dH}{db} = -b\, \mathrm{Var}_p(z), \qquad \frac{dH}{dT} = \frac{\mathrm{Var}_p(z)}{T^3} \geq 0 .
    $$

16. **★★ Compute-optimal allocation.** Minimise the scaling law of Definition 7.5 under the constraint $6ND = C$. Show that the optimal sizes grow as powers of the budget,
    $$
    N_{\mathrm{opt}} \propto C^{\beta / (\alpha + \beta)}, \qquad D_{\mathrm{opt}} \propto C^{\alpha / (\alpha + \beta)},
    $$
    and evaluate the exponents for the fitted values $\alpha = 0.34$ and $\beta = 0.28$ of Hoffmann and coauthors (2022).

    *Solution*: substitute $D = C / (6N)$ and set the derivative in $N$ to zero:
    $$
    \alpha A N^{-\alpha - 1} = \beta B\, 6^{\beta}\, C^{-\beta} N^{\beta - 1} \iff N^{\alpha + \beta} = \frac{\alpha A}{\beta B} \Big( \frac{C}{6} \Big)^{\beta} .
    $$

    Hence $a = \beta/(\alpha + \beta) \approx 0.45$ and $D = C/(6N)$ gives $b = 1 - a \approx 0.55$: parameters and tokens grow almost equally, unlike earlier recommendations that put most of the budget into parameters.

17. **★★★ Designing a human-parity study.** A company claims that its sentiment classifier “reaches human performance” because its accuracy against one annotator equals that of a second annotator. Using Proposition 12.2 and Code 12.5, write the protocol of a study that would support or refute the claim.

    *Hints and expected result*: several independent annotators with a stated profile; agreement measured by kappa before any comparison; systems and humans scored on the same items against an adjudicated reference, or against each annotator in turn; paired bootstrap intervals; an analysis of error types (negation, irony, neutral cases), since equal accuracy can hide different errors; a pre-registered decision rule. The expected conclusion is a statement with an interval, not a yes or no.

18. **★★★ Kneser–Ney against add-k (Python).** Generate 25,000 tokens from a Markov chain over 300 words with sparse, Zipf-shaped transition rows. Train on 20,000 tokens and compare the test perplexity of add-k smoothing (several $k$) and interpolated Kneser–Ney (several $d$).

    *Hints and expected result*: tune $k$ and $d$ on the test set only for this exercise; use a held-out set in practice.

    ```python
    import math
    import numpy as np
    from collections import Counter
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    V = 300                                                   # Markov text with Zipfian, sparse rows
    zipf = 1.0 / np.arange(1, V + 1)
    P = np.stack([rng.dirichlet(0.05 * V * zipf / zipf.sum()) for _ in range(V)])
    cdf = P.cumsum(1)
    x, u = [0], rng.random(25000)
    for t in range(25000):
        x.append(min(int(np.searchsorted(cdf[x[-1]], u[t])), V - 1))
    train, test = x[:20000], x[20000:]
    big = Counter(zip(train, train[1:])); ctx = Counter(train[:-1])
    fol = Counter(a for a, b in big); pre = Counter(b for a, b in big); n_types = len(big)

    def pp(prob):
        lp = [math.log(prob(b, a)) for a, b in zip(test, test[1:])]
        return math.exp(-sum(lp) / len(lp))

    def add_k(k):
        return lambda b, a: (big[a, b] + k) / (ctx[a] + k * V)

    def kn(d):
        def p(b, a):
            cont = (pre[b] + 0.5) / (n_types + 0.5 * V)       # smoothed continuation probability
            if ctx[a] == 0:
                return cont
            return max(big[a, b] - d, 0) / ctx[a] + d * fol[a] / ctx[a] * cont
        return p

    print("add-k :", {k: round(pp(add_k(k)), 1) for k in [1, 0.1, 0.03, 0.01]})
    print("KN    :", {d: round(pp(kn(d)), 1) for d in [0.5, 0.75, 0.9]})
    ```

    Add-k gives 35.9 for $k = 1$ and at best 21.1 for $k = 0.03$; Kneser–Ney gives 20.2 for $d = 0.5$. The continuation probability needs a small add-0.5 term here, because a test word may never have been seen as a second word.

19. **★★★ What do discrete speech units encode? (Python, research-flavoured.)** Spoken language models (ch. 14) cluster speech features into units. Synthesise the vowels /a/, /i/ and /u/ at three pitches with the source–filter generator of Code 2.7, compute MFCCs without $c_0$, cluster the frames by k-means with 3, 9 and 27 units, and measure the normalised mutual information of the units with the vowel and with the pitch.

    *Hints and expected result*:

    ```python
    import numpy as np
    from scipy.fft import dct
    from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
    from sklearn.metrics import normalized_mutual_info_score as nmi
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    sr, n_fft, win, hop = 16000, 512, 400, 160
    vowels = {"a": [700, 1200], "i": [300, 2300], "u": [300, 800]}   # first two formants (Hz)
    edges = 700 * (10 ** (np.linspace(0, 2595 * np.log10(1 + 8000 / 700), 42) / 2595) - 1)
    bins = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_fft, 1 / sr)
    fb = np.stack([np.clip(np.minimum((bins - edges[m]) / (edges[m + 1] - edges[m]),
                                      (edges[m + 2] - bins) / (edges[m + 2] - edges[m + 1])), 0, None) for m in range(40)])

    def mfcc_frames(f0, formants):
        t = np.arange(sr // 4) / sr
        x = sum(np.exp(-0.5 * ((h * f0 - np.array(formants)) / 100.0) ** 2).sum() * np.sin(2 * np.pi * h * f0 * t)
                for h in range(1, int(7000 / f0)))
        x = x + 0.01 * rng.normal(size=x.size)
        frames = np.stack([x[i: i + win] for i in range(0, len(x) - win, hop)]) * np.hamming(win)
        logmel = np.log(np.abs(np.fft.rfft(frames, n_fft)) ** 2 @ fb.T + 1e-8)
        return dct(logmel, norm="ortho", axis=1)[:, 1:13]           # drop c0 (loudness)

    X, vowel_lab, pitch_lab = [], [], []
    for vi, (v, F) in enumerate(vowels.items()):
        for pj, f0 in enumerate([100, 150, 220]):
            M = mfcc_frames(f0, F); X.append(M)
            vowel_lab += [vi] * len(M); pitch_lab += [pj] * len(M)
    for k in [3, 9, 27]:
        units = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(np.vstack(X))
        print(k, round(nmi(vowel_lab, units), 2), round(nmi(pitch_lab, units), 2))
    ```

    With 3 units the clusters are exactly the vowels (NMI 1.00 with the vowel, 0.00 with the pitch). With 9 units they also split by pitch (0.67 and 0.57), and with 27 units both are 0.52: finer units encode speaker properties along with phonetic content. The research question of ch. 14, 14.1, is how to keep the content and drop the rest; try adding noise, or speaker normalisation of the features.

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

The official assessment (master-mva.com) has two parts: online quizzes at the end of the classes, 40 % of the grade with the best 6 of 7 kept, and a final project, 60 %, done in groups of 2–4 around a recent speech or language processing paper with existing code. The project replicates the main result, then tests a new question; it is presented in a one-page plan, a 4-page report and a 10-minute talk with 5 minutes of questions, and graded individually.

The group subjects below follow this format; the solo subjects are smaller paper studies for practice; the written exam is a model of the comprehension questions.

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Word embeddings as matrix factorisation.** Is SGNS better than a well-tuned SVD of the PPMI matrix? A paper study of Levy, Goldberg and Dagan, “Improving Distributional Similarity with Lessons Learned from Word Embeddings” (TACL, 2015), building on Theorem 5.5.
    -   *Implement*: PPMI with context-distribution smoothing, truncated SVD, and SGNS (gensim), with matched windows and negative counts.
    -   *Data*: the text8 corpus (the first $10^8$ characters of a cleaned English Wikipedia dump); WordSim-353 (Finkelstein and coauthors, 2002) and SimLex-999 (Hill, Reichart and Korhonen, 2015) for evaluation.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. *Chapters*: ch. 0, 5.
    -   *Success*: Spearman correlations for both methods with bootstrap intervals; a check of Theorem 5.5 on frequent pairs; a verdict on the paper's claim that hyperparameters matter more than the algorithm.
2.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] A CTC recogniser for spoken digit strings.** How far does CTC go without any language model on a small vocabulary? A paper study of Graves and coauthors, “Connectionist Temporal Classification” (ICML, 2006).
    -   *Implement*: log-mel features (Code 2.7); a bidirectional LSTM trained with the CTC loss (Theorem 10.4); greedy and beam decoding.
    -   *Data*: the ten digit words of Speech Commands (Warden, 2018), concatenated into random strings of 3 to 7 digits with random pauses, with disjoint speakers for training and test.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. *Chapters*: ch. 2, 6, 10.
    -   *Success*: a digit-string error rate below 10 % on unseen speakers, and an analysis of the peaky behaviour of CTC posteriors (most frames emit the blank).
3.  **[Solo · ≈ 15 h] Neural text degeneration.** Does nucleus sampling produce text whose statistics are closest to human text? A paper study of Holtzman and coauthors, “The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration” (ICLR, 2020).
    -   *Implement*: greedy, beam ($B = 5$), pure, top-k ($k = 40$) and nucleus ($p = 0.95$) decoding (Definition 7.6) with GPT-2 small, from 200 prompts taken from WikiText-103 (Merity and coauthors, 2017).
    -   *Measure*: the share of repeated 4-grams, distinct-n, self-BLEU (Code 8.6) and the perplexity of the generations under a larger model.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4-page report. *Chapters*: ch. 7, 8, 12.
    -   *Success*: the paper's ordering reproduced (beam and greedy most repetitive, pure sampling least coherent, nucleus closest to human statistics), with bootstrap intervals over prompts.

### Group projects {#projects-group}

Each subject follows the official format: replicate the main result of the paper with its code, then test one new question; one-page plan first, then a 4-page report and a 10-minute talk.

1.  **[Group of 2–4 · ≈ 30 h each] Subword vocabularies for neural translation.** Replicate the BPE result of Sennrich, Haddow and Birch, “Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units” (ACL, 2016), with a small transformer.
    -   *Data and code*: IWSLT 2014 German→English (Cettolo and coauthors, 2014) with the fairseq toolkit (Ott and coauthors, 2019).
    -   *New question*: the effect of the number of merges, or of BPE-dropout (Provilkov, Emelianenko and Voita, 2020), on rare words and on a low-resource subset of 20,000 pairs.
    -   *Split*: data and tokenisation; training; evaluation (sacreBLEU, chrF, COMET, paired bootstrap) and error analysis; with four members, a human evaluation of 100 sentences.
    -   *Success*: a baseline within 2 BLEU points of the score reported by the fairseq IWSLT'14 example, and a significance-tested answer to the new question. *Chapters*: ch. 1, 6, 8, 12.
2.  **[Group of 2–4 · ≈ 30 h each] Where do fine-tuned transformers beat linear sentiment models?** Replicate the SST-2 accuracy of DistilBERT (Sanh and coauthors, 2019), against the NB-SVM baseline of Wang and Manning (ACL, 2012).
    -   *Data*: SST-2 (Socher and coauthors, 2013) and IMDB reviews (Maas and coauthors, 2011).
    -   *New question*: accuracy on sentences with negation or contrast (“but”), robustness to typos, and transfer from one dataset to the other.
    -   *Split*: baselines (ch. 9); fine-tuning (ch. 7); challenge sets and statistics (ch. 12).
    -   *Success*: development accuracy within 1 point of the paper; the gap on the negation subset with a bootstrap interval; a reasoned answer to “is the gain composition or vocabulary?”.
3.  **[Group of 3–4 · ≈ 30 h each] Sampling, pass@k and self-repair for code.** Replicate the pass@k curves of Chen and coauthors, “Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code” (2021), with an open code model of at most 1.5 billion parameters on a free GPU tier.
    -   *Data*: HumanEval and MBPP (Austin and coauthors, 2021).
    -   *New question*: does an agent loop with execution feedback (Definition 11.7) beat independent sampling at an equal budget of model calls? Compare with the analysis of Olausson and coauthors (ICLR, 2024).
    -   *Split*: sandboxed execution and the estimator (Proposition 11.5); sampling sweeps over temperature; the repair loop; analysis.
    -   *Success*: pass@1 within 2 points of the value reported for the chosen model; the paper's finding that the best temperature grows with $k$; the repair gain at equal budget, with intervals. *Chapters*: ch. 7, 11, 12.
4.  **[Group of 2–4 · ≈ 30 h each] Self-supervised speech with ten minutes of labels.** Replicate a low-resource row of wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski and coauthors, NeurIPS 2020): fine-tune the pretrained base model with CTC on the 10-minute or 1-hour split of Libri-light (Kahn and coauthors, 2020).
    -   *Evaluate*: WER on LibriSpeech test-clean and test-other (Panayotov and coauthors, 2015), without and with an n-gram language model.
    -   *New question*: which layers of the frozen model carry phonetic information (linear probes per layer), or how WER degrades with added noise.
    -   *Split*: fine-tuning; decoding with and without LM; probing and analysis.
    -   *Success*: WER within 20 % (relative) of the paper's value for the same split and decoding setting, and a layer-wise probe curve. *Chapters*: ch. 2, 10, 12.

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

Two hours, one handwritten A4 sheet allowed, no electronic device; four questions, 20 points. The questions mirror the comprehension quizzes of the official assessment, with one computation and one proof.

1.  **Question (4 points).** Compare the HMM tagger, the linear-chain CRF and CTC: what each one models, which independence assumption it makes, and which dynamic program computes its likelihood or normaliser.

    *Expected*:

    -   HMM: a joint law of tags and words; tags form a Markov chain and each word depends only on its tag; forward algorithm (1 pt).
    -   CRF: a conditional law of tags given the whole sentence; Markov in the tags, arbitrary features of the input; forward algorithm for $Z(x)$, concave likelihood (1.5 pts).
    -   CTC: a conditional law of a label sequence given frames, frame outputs independent given the input, alignments summed by the forward recursion on the label sequence extended with blanks (1.5 pts).
2.  **Question (6 points).** (a) An HMM over the symbols $x$ and $y$ has two states, and
    $$
    \pi = (0.5, 0.5), \qquad A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.3 \\ 0.4 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad P(x \mid 1) = 0.9, \quad P(x \mid 2) = 0.2 .
    $$
    For the observations $x, y$, compute $P(O)$ and the best path. (b) Compute BLEU with $N = 1$ for the hypothesis “the the cat” against the reference “the cat sat on the mat”. (c) Compute the WER of “turn lights of” against “turn the lights off”.

    *Expected*:

    -   (a) $\alpha_1 = (0.45, 0.10)$ and $\alpha_2 = (0.0355, 0.156)$, so $P(O) = 0.1915$; $\delta_2 = (0.0315, 0.108)$, best path 1 then 2, of probability 0.108 (3 pts).
    -   (b) Clipped precision $3/3 = 1$, but the hypothesis has 3 words against 6, so $\mathrm{BP} = e^{1 - 6/3} \approx 0.368$ and BLEU-1 is 0.368 (1.5 pts).
    -   (c) One deletion (“the”) and one substitution (“off” → “of”) on 4 words: 50 % (1.5 pts).
3.  **Question (5 points).** Prove Theorem 5.5: if each inner product can be set freely, the SGNS objective summed over the corpus is maximised at $\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{u} = \mathrm{PMI}(w, u) - \log k$.

    *Expected*:

    -   The pair is drawn as a negative $k\, c(w)\, c(u) / D$ times in expectation, so the objective is a sum over pairs of (2 pts)
        $$
        \ell(s) = c(w, u) \log \sigma(s) + \frac{k\, c(w)\, c(u)}{D} \log \sigma(-s) .
        $$
    -   With $\sigma' = \sigma(s)\sigma(-s)$, setting $\ell'(s) = 0$ gives $e^s = c(w, u) D / (k\, c(w) c(u))$ (2 pts).
    -   Each $\ell$ is strictly concave, so this is the maximum, and the pairs decouple (1 pt).
4.  **Question (5 points).** (a) Show that if $q, k \in \mathbb{R}^d$ have independent entries of mean 0 and variance 1, then $\mathrm{Var}(q^\top k) = d$, and explain the factor $1/\sqrt{d}$. (b) With $d = 2$, compute the two outputs of causal scaled dot-product attention for
    $$
    q_1 = (1, 0),\ q_2 = (0, 1), \qquad k_1 = (1, 1),\ k_2 = (1, -1), \qquad v_1 = (1, 0),\ v_2 = (0, 1) .
    $$
    (c) Why do transformers need positional information?

    *Expected*:

    -   (a) A sum of $d$ independent terms of mean 0 and variance 1; unscaled scores saturate the softmax (1.5 pts).
    -   (b) Position 1 sees only itself: output $v_1 = (1, 0)$. Position 2 has scores $\pm 1/\sqrt{2}$, weights $(0.804, 0.196)$, output $(0.804, 0.196)$ (2 pts).
    -   (c) Without a mask or positions, self-attention is permutation-equivariant (Proposition 6.7), so “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” would get the same multiset of outputs (1.5 pts).

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

The rubric follows the official requirements of the project: a plan, a replication, a new question, a report, a talk and individual grading.

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Plan and organisation | 10 % | A one-page plan with a precise question, a schedule and a split of the work, delivered on time |
| Replication | 25 % | The main result of the paper reproduced with its code, discrepancies measured and explained |
| New question | 20 % | A new task, dataset or variant that tests something the paper did not, motivated by the course |
| Evaluation and analysis | 15 % | Correct metrics (ch. 1, 4, 8, 10, 11), several seeds or bootstrap intervals, error analysis, negative results reported |
| Report | 10 % | Four clear pages: question, method, results with uncertainty, limits |
| Talk and questions | 10 % | Ten minutes on time, readable figures, precise answers in the 5 minutes of questions |
| Individual engagement | 10 % | Each member's contribution visible in the plan, the code history and the answers to questions |
